utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number IT-98-32-T, the Prosecutor versus Mitar Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sir, would you please make the statutory declaration in the document which the usher is showing you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sit down, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Have we got a new list of witnesses for this week, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, unfortunately, this is the last witness who has come to The Hague. The remaining two witnesses, that is to say, Dr. Djordje Stojkovic and the witness from Visegrad for whom we requested protective measures - so I don't want to mention his name although you know who he is - unfortunately, they have not arrived, despite all our attempts over the weekend to have them come. Dr. Stojkovic has said that, unfortunately, he is unable to come before mid-December because of prior engagements, and that was also the reason given by the other witness, so that we are faced with the situation in which these two remaining witnesses have not arrived. On the list, there was also Witness Pecikoza, and we gave up on him quite a while ago because he said that he did not wish to come so that we didn't, in fact, call him. But the other two witnesses whose passports are with the offices in Sarajevo are unfortunately unable to make it at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, we'll worry about what we can do about those two in a moment. Obviously, we don't need a list if this is the only one you have at the moment. Let's get on with this witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can I start? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Dr. Moljevic.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Dr. Moljevic, I will be examining you on behalf of the Defence team but let me caution you that, as we speak the same language, you and I, please make pauses between my questions and your answers. And the monitor in front of will you help you see when the translation has been completed and I shall do the same to facilitate the work of the interpreters. I should like to ask you first and foremost to introduce yourself to the Court, tell us your name and surname, your place and date of birth, and other particulars.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I have a question. Do I have to get up or can I answer sitting down?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No, you may remain seated.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, distinguished Judges, the Prosecution, the lawyers and everybody else in the courtroom, my name is Dr. Aleksandar Moljevic. I was born in 1956, on the 23rd of September, in Cacak, the Republic of Serbia. By profession, I am a doctor. I am a specialist in orthopaedic surgery and traumatology and my working title is primarius. My work post is head of department for traumatology of the orthopaedic department at the general hospital at Uzice.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Moljevic, will you tell us since when you have been working at the general hospital in Uzice in the department you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I have been working at the department for orthopaedic surgery and traumatology at the Uzice general hospital since the 1st of February, 1987, when I started my specialist training, and completed my specialist training on the 8th of March, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Where did you work before that, Dr. Moljevic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I worked in the health clinic of Visegrad or health centre. I think it was from February 1983.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you began working in Visegrad, until your arrival in Uzice, did you work in Visegrad continuously throughout that time?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, except for a period of less than one year when I did my military service, and that was in 1984, between 1984 and 1985.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Since you have been in Uzice onwards, did you spend part of your time working in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understood you. You mean before I completed my specialist training or while I was doing my specialist training?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Generally speaking, since you have been working in Uzice, did you have occasion from time to time to go to Visegrad, rather, do you have days when you see patients in Visegrad or days when you are on duty in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have a private practice in Visegrad and I examine patients once a week. I'm on duty there and perform minor surgical interventions. Before that, I would go to -- I would visit health centres in the region and this was a contract that the Uzice general hospital had with these health centres, and for a time that contract included cooperation with the Visegrad health centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In view of the time you spent working in Visegrad while you were in Uzice and later on, means that you know Visegrad very well and the people of the town; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Moljevic, let me go back to -- let me focus on what we're interested in here and that is the year 1982, and as you said, you were in the hospital in Uzice. Would you recall that period of May, 1992 - 1992 - what you did at that time and how your department functioned within the general hospital when tensions already existed and the conflicts began?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Up until the middle of March 1992, I was involved as a reserve sanitary officer, we used to call it, a surgeon in the military medical corps. From mid-March, I was in my hospital of Titovo Uzice. It was called Titovo Uzice at the time, and I remember the period when the first wounded and injured came in from the newly-opened front in Bosnia. The Uzice general hospital and the town of Uzice itself is about 70 kilometres away from Visegrad and about 40 kilometres away from Skelani, which are two of the nearest towns in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the patients and inhabitants from those towns gravitate towards Uzice for treatment, that is to say, they come to Uzice for treatment because our hospital is the largest regional hospital in Serbia and we have about 1.000 beds. At the beginning of the war, we admitted all persons who were wounded and injured, that is to say, soldiers and civilians alike regardless of their ethnic affiliation or the army they belonged to or their military unit. As a surgeon myself, I was one of the more experienced people in the area of surgery. I was already an experienced surgeon, and as I have told you from before, I had been engaged as a reserve officer, a surgeon in the medical corps of the then Yugoslav Peoples' Army. If you were to ask me in greater detail or some specific questions, I would be able to answer you like this. I don't know what you want me to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Dr. Moljevic, as you remember the period well, I am interested to know whether, within the frameworks of your hospital, you changed your method of work with respect to the admission of patients and triage of patients because you had this great influx of injured and wounded compared to the procedure you applied before that. So what was your procedure from April onwards in 1992?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I was watching the screen. In April 1992, when the conflict had broken out in Bosnia-Herzegovina and with a greater influx of wounded and injured persons, people coming to our hospital, the administration in the hospital introduced extraordinary measures, a state of alert for work in the hospital, and that state of alert implied a maximum reduction of -- that is to say, cutting down patients' admissions to all hospital departments except the pediatric department and gynecology. All the other departments, in view of their capacities, were placed at the disposal and at the service of surgical disorders and surgery. Generally speaking, the accent was placed on surgery, so that our department, too, was subordinated to the surgical department. At the admissions department, what we called a triage team was set up and the head of that team was an experienced surgeon, one of the experienced surgeons of what we call the surgical group of the department, and that was made up of general surgery with its subsections: chest surgery, abdominal surgery, neurosurgery. Next, there was children's surgery as a separate department, as a separate section. Then we had the orthopaedics department with its subsections for orthopaedics and traumatology, and the department for maxilofacial and otorhinolaryngology and the eye department. In the admissions triage team, as I have said, the head of the team was always one of our experienced surgeons, whether an orthopaedic surgeon, surgeon, and one colleague at that time who was head of child surgery and he was also a general surgeon with vast experience in the field of surgery. I was one of the surgeons who, if I was not actually operating in the operating theatre, I was, in the ensuing period or as my regular work, engaged as head of the triage team. So that roughly was the hospital organisation at the start of the war and conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Later on, we adjusted and restructured this as the need arose and based on the experience we had gained.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: During this -- the existence of the admissions triage team, could you tell us what the procedure was like when a patient came from the war zone and he was injured? Where would the patient come, what did the triage team do, where would the patient be forwarded to, et cetera? Tell us a little about that, please, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Upon arrival to the hospital at the entrance to the emergency -- at the emergency entrance, once the patient was transported on a stretcher into the hospital, he would be sent to room number 8 - I think it was room number 8 -- at the admissions department. It is a large room with all the necessary equipment for resuscitation, reanimation for stopping bleeding and for administering first aid and emergency medical assistance, including an internist part with a cardiac arrest. Usually, the doctor at the admissions department, who is a general practitioner, calls in a surgeon or the head or chief of the triage team if the patient is seriously wounded and is also bleeding. If the doctor thinks that the injury is not life threatening, then he, himself, issues orders as to how the patient should be treated further in the sense of issuing orders for radiography, x-rays, x-rays of the injured extremities. It might be the head, the chest, or the abdomen. He takes a basic laboratory test, performs basic laboratory tests, which means the blood picture, haematocrits, glucemia, urine, urea, and creatine. Next, he would do an EKG, that is to say an electrocardiogram, and once all these required results are obtained from the tests conducted, he would call in either the chief of the triage team or a doctor of the required specialty from the triage team because in the triage team, except for the surgeon who was always chief of the team, there was always a surgeon. We would also have an internal medicine specialist as well as an infectologist or, upon requirement, another specialist depending on who made up the team on that particular day. If the patient has injured his extremities, then we would call for an orthopaedist who is on duty 24 hours round the clock at the orthopaedic department and comes down to the admissions department when he is called. Similarly, we would call in other doctors who are on duty, who are doing duty in their own departments, according to the same principle. The principle would always be the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Moljevic.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You mentioned the doctor on duty. Does that mean that independently of the triage team that you described, each separate department also had a doctor on duty who would be on duty in the afternoon and during the night when the first shift was off duty? Was that how the hospital was organised?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. All our hospital departments have doctors on duty 24 hours round the clock. A specialist would be on duty round the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could you tell me, please, Dr. Moljevic, for the period we are discussing, who worked in your own department, that is to say the orthopaedic department, and were they orthopaedic surgeons or what profile?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: You mean that day or generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: At the orthopaedic department of the general hospital at that time, the head of the department was primarius Dr. Dragoslav Milosavijevic, who is now retired. Then there was primarius Dr. Primisav Spanusavuvic [phoen], emeritus professor and my late chief. Then we had primarius Dr. Dusko Pribicevic. At the time he was the director of the general hospital. Then there was Dr. Djordje Stojkovic, the head of the department at the moment. He is my department head at present. Then there was Dr. Vojkan Krnic, who works in the Cacak hospital, and then there was myself. Dr. Zoran Stojanovic, as well, who is now working in Plandiste in Vojvodina. Then there was Dr. Ivan Jovanovic. He was a doctor doing specialised training at the time in the sphere of orthopaedics and traumatology, and there is Dr. Vladimir Gordic who at that time is what we call the secondary doctor, that is to say a general practitioner preparing to do his specialist training at the orthopaedics department and traumatology department. I think I have enumerated them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. To go back to the hospital at this particular period of time, my next question is the following: Did you know Mitar Vasiljevic from Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could you tell us, please, since when have you known him and how did you come to know him?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Mitar Vasiljevic was a waiter in the hotel catering company called Panos of Visegrad. Usually, he worked on the terrace of the Visegrad hotel and I think a section, a bar, there that was called Panos. I knew him since the time I received permission from my father to be able to frequent restaurants and bars. I think I happened to notice him at that time, but we didn't actually know each other until I had graduated from university and started working in Visegrad. At that time, I went to restaurants and bars more often because I had more money to spend on things like that. So that my friends and the people I socialised with, usually after work, especially on Fridays and Saturdays, would go out to dinner and to listen to music to a lovely terrace of the Visegrad hotel. Mitar Vasiljevic was very often on duty there and served our table. He was a very good waiter and I can also tell you that the other waiters, usually older waiters who would serve us, I assume would serve our table more frequently because we would give generous tips generally in bars and restaurants.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Moljevic. Let me just ask you something. From your answer, it appears to me that you were in Visegrad before you graduated, but in your answer, you said that you began working there and you were born, as I see, in Cacak. Could you tell us since when have you been in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: My mother had what we call a high-risk pregnancy so that she gave birth to me in the Cacak hospital because Visegrad at the time did not have a gynecologist. So I was only born in Cacak actually, but I spent my entire life until I left for Uzice living in Visegrad. That is to say my childhood, I did primary school there, secondary school, college and until I left for university. So I lived in Visegrad until I left to go to university, and to this very day, I'm there very frequently because my parents live in Visegrad, as does practically the whole of my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Moljevic. I think we have managed to cover something that we actually left out before. Let us go back to Mitar Vasiljevic and I should like to hear you, how it was that you knew him. What you said about him, does that concern the period of time that you spent living in Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Except for the fact that you saw him from time to time as a waiter in the restaurants where he served, did you personally have any contacts with his family? Did you visit that family? Did the members of that family come to your house?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Moljevic, let us go back to the period of time that you described in the Uzice hospital that is following the month of April 1992. Do you remember Mitar Vasiljevic from that period of time as a patient of that hospital?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember him quite well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you please tell us what it is that you remember, including the time that you first saw him and everything else that you remember from that period?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Mitar Vasiljevic was admitted to our hospital pursuant to some medical documents on the 14th of June, in the evening hours of the 14th of June. He had a fracture of the left lower leg. On that day, I happened to be the chief of the admissions triage team and before he came to hospital, someone had called me from Visegrad, I don't remember who it was, but it was for the second or the third time that day because we had had several admissions from that particular area, telling me that the injured -- that an injured person by the name of Vasiljevic is arriving. I was informed by the admissions department doctors that he had arrived because the call was addressed to me, and at that time, I was at the orthopaedics department where I saw an injured a wounded person and dressed his wounds, who happened to be a neighbour and who was also the brother of a man with whom I went to school and a son of a very good friend of my father. At the admissions department in room number eight which was established for such cases, there was Vasiljevic. He was on a stretcher. Next to him there was a driver by the name of Zivorad Savic, whom I knew from Visegrad because he was the driver in my shift of the emergency department in Visegrad where I worked. And since the injury in question was a fracture of a lower leg, I sent him to my colleague Ivicovic [phoen] for further treatment because we were already busy with something else. So up until the next morning, I no longer saw him because I didn't go back to the orthopaedics department that night. On the basis of the medical documentation and in view of my capacity here as a witness before The Hague Tribunal, I checked the day and was able to establish that it was a Sunday. The following day, that is on Monday, after the usual briefing that I had with the director of the hospital which starts at 7.00 a.m. and lasts for 20 minutes, I went to inspect the patients. It is the main round of inspection which is carried out with the head doctor, usually on Monday at 7.30. I cannot remember the particular room that Vasiljevic was in on that day. What I am certain about, on the other hand, is that the remainder period of time while he was in hospital, he was in room number 411, 4-1-1. That is the first room located in the right wing of our department, and my colleague, Dr. Primarius Ivicovic is in charge of that particular room. After a while, we observed the unusual behaviour of Vasiljevic and the doctors who were on duty were told that this unusual behaviour consisted of singing, sticking some drawings and photographs all over the wall - which is forbidden at the department and he was consequently warned to take that off - and this behaviour was also characterised by an incident involving another patient by the name of Selim Lepenica, a Muslim who was a civilian victim of the war and was from Gorazde. He displayed aggressive behaviour towards that patient, and according to our knowledge, he tried to hit him with a stick while lying -- with his crutch, while lying in his bed. He verbally abused him and because of that, he was told and warned that in case of other violations of the house rules and regulations, appropriate measures would be applied, that is, that he would be discharged prematurely or taken to the psychiatry ward. His transfer to the psychiatry department is a subject matter that I'm not able to tell you about because I was not there. However, judging from the dates, I know that it happened between the weekend of the 5th of July and the national holiday which was celebrated in our country in those days on the 7th of July. That is what I can tell you about his transfer to the psychiatric department and his admission there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: That is what I can tell you, excuse me, about his stay at the orthopaedics department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think this doctor is about the closest we've got to the first doctor who saw your client when he was admitted, Dr. Jovanovic, I think is his name. Now all we've heard from this witness is that your client was admitted during the evening hours, I think was the expression. I think, if I may say so, we are somewhat concerned to know when he saw him and where he fits in with the doctor who actually signed the papers as having admitted your client. This is an issue which the Prosecution has raised and it would be best, if I may suggest, that you take the witness to that particular issue so that we get some assistance from it. He's clearly someone who can assist us on that issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I do intend to ask that, but I believe that Dr. Moljevic described on his own initiative the stay of Vasiljevic in that particular department, which was supposed to be the subject of my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: But I should like to focus on the admission and go back to the evening when you said you were a member of the admissions triage team on duty. Let us try to clarify that and then perhaps we will go back to Vasiljevic's stay at the orthopaedics department, if necessary. What is important for us is to know when exactly it was that Mitar Vasiljevic was admitted to your hospital. I should like to know whether such records are usually kept, whether there was a ledger, a book which would have included cases like these, that is, the cases of people who were brought from the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: There is a big book at the admissions department which contains records on all cases admitted to the hospital regardless of the department in question. However, it seems to me that in those days, we also had an additional book where we kept records of the wounded and the injured from the area of the former Yugoslavia because in 1991, we admitted other cases as well. In that book, there would be the name and the surname of the patient, the diagnosis on arrival, the name of the driver of the ambulance which brought the patient to the hospital, and the department to which the patient was eventually admitted. Once the patient is admitted at the admissions department, that is when the doctor decides on the department where he would be admitted, the procedure is carried out by the administrative and technical staff who enter the relevant data on the first page of the case history, whereupon the patient is transported or transferred to the department to which he or she is to be admitted. Once at the department of admission, the identifying data of the patient are entered in the department book of admissions. As for the case history document, in the upper right corner, the name of the room where the patient was admitted is usually -- the number of the room, I'm sorry, where the patient was admitted is usually entered and the name of the doctor, the specialist who is to be in charge of further treatment of the patient. So once the patient has left the admissions department, any interest of the members in that department in that patient ceases because he is taken over by another part in the hospital, the department that is to be in charge of his treatment, and that is the situation until the end of his stay, the patient's stay at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Dr. Moljevic, let us go back to the admissions department and the book that you described which contained the data of those who had been injured or wounded in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. You stated that the data entered in that book include also the name of the driver who had brought the patient, the diagnosis as well, and I should like to know whether the time of admission, in addition to the date, is also entered in that book, the time, that is the hour and the minute of admission?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, on a regular basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, I don't like to interrupt, but we don't have any such book, do we? I can remember there was a --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: A book with the date. Does it have a time?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, that book was seized and is in the possession of the Prosecutor since the 1st of November last year, together with all other remaining documents. That book is one of such documents that were seized during the search and I ask the Prosecutor to prepare that book for us so that the witness could have a look at it and testify as to whether that is the book in question. I think the book is blue or dark red. There was one blue book and another one which was dark red, burgundy in colour. I inspected it several days ago. I think that we should show it to the witness; however, I should like to ask a question before that, a question relating to the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It is, so far as I know, not in evidence, although in a document somewhere, there was a -- just a strip and it just had your client's name and the date of his admission, not the time, and we had nothing above it or below it. I don't think even the -- I do not think that even that document is in evidence. So there was no way of judging even approximately the time he came in. Now, there's one that we have a photostat of. I don't know quite what its provenance is, it's not yet in evidence, which does show a time, but I think we're going to have some help. It just can't be overlooked. We've got to have some assistance on this particular issue. So we need every book that has any relevance to time of admission and we need more than that just little strip that we were shown before. So if you just see what you can do to get them into evidence. It's your case, remember. I know you bear no onus but you are the one seeking to demonstrate the reasonableness of the possibility that your client was in hospital at the time that this crime was alleged to have been committed. I'm sorry, it is in -- now in evidence as part of 137.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I provided a photocopy of what you say that contained nothing above or below because that was the kind of copy that I received at the hospital. It was a certified copy; however, at that time, they did not want to photocopy the portions of the text including other names, names of other patients. They gave me only the data concerning Vasiljevic and that is what I provided. The time is also stated there in addition to the date. However, the original of the book was brought by Dr. Moljevic to the Prosecutor, which material was seized pursuant to an order of the Tribunal and is now in possession of the Prosecutor, and it is very important for us that that book be examined and for the witness to be given an opportunity to comment on the book. By comparison, you will be able to see that that indeed was the copy that I provided but the copy concerned only Mitar Vasiljevic. I kindly ask the Prosecutor to have the book in the courtroom. I think that Mr. Ossogo or -- is it there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, well you proceed with that but don't forget that we'd like to know if this witness can tell us when it was that he first saw him and whether it was before or after the other doctor signed him in as a patient.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not yet, Dr. Moljevic. Before we have a look at any of these books, Dr. Moljevic, I have a question for you concerning a patient that you said you had seen on that day and who had been admitted to hospital and you said that he was a neighbour of yours. Is that the individual who was admitted to hospital before Mitar Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, and he's from Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could you tell us his name and surname, please?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: The name of that patient was Dragan Filipovic. He's deceased, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Was he also brought from the town of Visegrad as an injured or wounded person?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: He'd been wounded as a soldier in his right shoulder, and in view of the wound and the graft that I applied during his treatment, I was able to recognise him during an identification of dead bodies including his body -- in a later period of time during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Dr. Moljevic, you have told us about what you remember. You said that Mitar Vasiljevic was admitted in the evening hours of that day. Would you please try and remember the exact time of his admission? And you also mentioned another doctor who was the first person who saw Mitar Vasiljevic when he arrived in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I spoke in general terms. I said that he was admitted in the evening hours, that is how we usually say. It was already night. I believe that it was around 9.30 p.m. because I also based my statement on some documents that I inspected. So I think that he was admitted around 2130. The physician who was there at the admissions department, the general practitioner, I cannot remember who it was because those teams were sent -- were established on the previous day, either through an oral order or a written order issued by the chief surgeon of the hospital who was in charge of selecting members of the team for a particular day.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Dr. Moljevic, you are referring to the doctor who was at the admissions department?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: However, I should like to know which of the orthopaedists was the first one who had contact with Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, since I am an orthopaedist, I was the first one who saw him but it was my colleague, Dr. Ivicovic, who was in charge of his further treatment because he was on duty in the orthopaedics department on that day. I believe you understand me. If a surgeon had been in my place, then that surgeon would have seen him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, that was my question. So you saw him and then Dr. Jovicovic saw him. I see that in the transcript it says "Ivicovic" but the name is Jovicovic. You said, Dr. Moljevic, that Dr. Jovicovic was on duty at the orthopaedics department. Was he the doctor who was in fact on duty during the second and third shift, that is to say the afternoon and during the night up until the morning; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, but an orthopaedist starts to go on duty -- for example, my duty shift starts at 7.00 in the morning and finishes 7.00 a.m. the next morning. All admissions are taken down in my name, my name is put down whether I see the patient or not or whether I see him just when he gets to the department. If, in the meantime, I'm off operating in the operating theatre or if I am an assistant to a surgeon in the operating theatre, that is what our practice has been.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Is that the reason why Mr. Mitar Vasiljevic was written down as being Dr. Jovicovic's patient both in the card and in the room he was assigned to later on?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Dr. Moljevic, when you were explaining what the procedure is for urgent cases, in general terms, you talked about the tests and analyses that are taken straight away. Do you happen to remember for this particular case, the case of Mitar Vasiljevic, was he sent to any other control examination, laboratory tests, any screening or anything like that when -- since the time he was admitted at the -- in the admissions department until he was transferred to the ward? If you happen to remember that, between his admission and the time he was sent to the ward.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember. I really don't remember because a lot of time has gone by since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Do you happen to remember, Dr. Moljevic, whether on that occasion, Mitar Vasiljevic had with him an x-ray of his injury? Do you happen to remember having seen that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I do not remember because the x-rays are brought to me by the technician or the doctor at the admissions department. Whether the patient brought them with him or whether the x-rays were done in my hospital, I can't really say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said, Dr. Moljevic, that the technician at the admissions department fills in part of the case history. He puts in the date and takes down the general particulars and that goes with the patient to the ward. My question now is whether, at the admissions department, the patient is assigned an individual patient's number?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. All that is done at the admissions department. In our department, we have nothing to do with that kind of administration so the patient is assigned a personal identification number.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Is that number recorded in the case history which follows the patient, and is it recorded in any other book or ledger of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and we call it the personal identification number, which is in the upper right-hand corner. I'd have to have a look at the case history form to be sure whether it is under one, two or three. Whereas all the other investigations and tests that we require in our department, it is compulsory to have the name, the surname, what is being requested, what types of tests, and all those sheets and lists contain the personal identification number of the patient to avoid any errors in the writing of names and surnames because that happens even today. Sometimes mistakes are made in writing the names, but if we have the personal identification number, we will know exactly which patient it is. This is particularly important for blood tests as preparation for operations. So let me repeat, we always have the personal identification number which can be compared in all the various documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Dr. Moljevic, I think that this is an opportune moment for you to take a look at the books in front of you and tell us if you see the book which was used in the admissions department for recording the patients that were admitted. If that is the notebook, Doctor, would you look at the hard cover and tell us what it says as the title on the hard cover?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: This thick book here is the book of admissions, all patients admitted, not only those who were injured or wounded but all patients coming into the hospital. It is in alphabetical order and it says "1992" on it. This other thinner book is the book of admissions for patients from the war zone, from the -- and it is dated the 6th of April, 1992 onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And was that the book you were reading from?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I handed it over in a proper and correct state.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you read out, doctor, please, what it says on the hard cover of that thin book? The book you are holding in your right hand.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Book of patients from the war zone or battlefield, the date is the 6th of April, 1992. In the upper right hand corner, it says admissions or in the neuter gender, "priljem," admissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you open that book, please, and you can put the other one aside for the time being.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Do we know which one would be likely to be filled in first? I don't think the doctor has told us that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Let us ask the doctor. Of the two books, Doctor -- Dr. Moljevic, you have two books in front of you. Which book is filled in first; do you know?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know and I don't think it is significant whether it is one or the other. Both are at the reception department. Now, whether the technician takes hold of one book first or this other one, I don't think it is important, At least, not for our purposes. I apologise, it's not of importance for our purposes in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The two books differ as to the information that is recorded in them; is that right? Looking at the one in front of you now, and looking at the columns, it doesn't matter what patient, just select a random patient and tell us what information is recorded in the book and then we'll see what information is written down in the other book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: He's dealing with the one now with the patients from the war zone? I can't see because of the screen in front of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes, Your Honour. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you look at the 14th of June, 1992? Perhaps that would be best if we take a look at that date.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I have found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: At the top, it says the title of each column, what each column contains. So would you read slowly, please, read through the columns and tell us what information should be recorded there and then we'll see what is actually recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it is Exhibit 137, which I think you have. It is a Prosecution Exhibit and I think that we have that particular page, the page that the witness is looking at now.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: May I begin?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please, Doctor. [In English] Have you? Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, I've got 137 and that's the thin book, and that's all I need to know, and then we'll go to the thick book.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Doctor, would you please take a look at the columns, the top of the columns, and read out what columns exist in the book first.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: In the book that is in front of me, the columns are as follows, and I'm moving from left to right: The first column says ordinal number; the second, date and time; the third, name and surname, first and last name; the fourth, the date and place of birth for the patient; next is the diagnosis; and then it says who brought the patient in. The next column is where he was admitted and what is referred to here is the hospital department. The next column, it says who the patient is, a soldier of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army belonging to his own Territorial Defence or civilian. And the last column it says "report," and it says -- the column says who has been informed about the patient's admission into our hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you now look and see which patients are written in that day, in the date and time column? Does it always state the time?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the first patient the name and surname is Simo Vuleta, and the number is 186. The date is the 14th of June 1992 at 1430 hours. The third column, it says born 1935 in Vogosca. The fourth column diagnosis: ulcus bulbi duodeni sanguinems [phoen], which means a bleeding ulcer of the duodenum. Who brought the patient in, in that column, it says, "came on his own." Where he was admitted, it says, "admitted to the internal medicine department two," which is where the gastroenterology department is. Then we come to the next column, what he was at the time, civilian TO or JNA, it has a question mark. Probably, there were no particulars about that. And in the report, it says that they were compulsory -- that compulsorily informed whether regional department of the SUP Uzice, Republic of Serbia. It says military police and the responsible corps on the territory of Western Serbia, and also we find the number 985. I can't remember, but I seem to -- actually, I think it was the service for information and alert, whether for the town or for the department in the ministry of internal affairs, but I think that's what the 985 figure referred to. That was the first patient. The second was Filipovic Dragan, the same day he was admitted at 1540, and the third was Vasiljevic Mitar and here we see the time, which is 2135 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you read out what it says for Mitar Vasiljevic from start to finish, please, what you are able to read, if you can read the handwriting.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: In the column for Vasiljevic Mitar, it says quite literally as follows: Ordinal number 188. The date and time of admission, the 14.6.92 at 2135. The name and surname, Vasiljevic Mitar. The date and place of birth, 1954 Visegrad. The diagnosis, fractura tibia at fibula l. sin. That means a fracture of the tibia and fibula of the left leg. Who brought the patient to the hospital: Brought by the ambulance from Visegrad, the ambulance driver Savic Milorad. That's what it says here but I think the first man's name was "Zivorad," so this is a mistake in the first name of the driver, the mistake made by the administrator at the reception department. Where was he admitted, he was admitted to the orthopaedics department. Who he is, and where -- who is he and where was he assigned to at the time, it says TO Visegrad, Territorial Defence. And report, informed the secretariat of internal affairs, military police, 985.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Dr. Moljevic, is that the book that you recognise as being the book in which the persons wounded or injured in the war zone or on the battlefield were recorded?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely correct, that is the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The patient who is in front of Mitar Vasiljevic who comes before, is that the one that you described as being your neighbour from Visegrad whom you knew and whom you visited and whom you described?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. He is the late Dragan Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Before we take a look at the other book, and in order to check that information and the way in which facts have been recorded, I would like to ask you to look at the 24th of June now of that same year, so that is several pages later on, and see if there is a patient by the name of Goran Loncarevic and if -- would you read out his particulars, please? What day was he admitted and when?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise for smiling, for laughing. It is a colleague of mine, a doctor, so my -- I don't want it to appear as if we're sidetracking. 228 is the number. The person -- he was admitted at 7.30 hours on the 24th of June. The name is Goran Loncarevic, born 1962 in Visegrad. The diagnosis is vulnus scapuloterium verasis l. dex [phoen], which in translation means bullet wound to the right side of the chest. He was brought from Visegrad by ambulance. The driver's name is Zivorad, I assume the same man, Savic, and he was admitted. It says shock, surgical shock. He belonged to the Territorial Defence of Visegrad, and informed were the military police, the secretariat for internal affairs, and number 985.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that you recognise the name and the person to be your colleague. Do you happen to know how he was wounded?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: There was never any issue about this, Mr. Domazet. I don't think we need to have this gone into again. The doctor -- that doctor was not cross-examined to suggest he was not telling the truth about his injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I asked the question, Your Honour, because of the method in which it was recorded in the book. So let me rephrase my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Dr. Moljevic, you, yourself, read out the hard cover of the book where it said that it was patients admitted from the war zone, the ratiste. What did the concept of war zone or battlefield imply as relevant to the book?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: It was the customary term or slang, perhaps somebody from the hospital administration thought it up, and that was what we wrote. Now, why it said "ratiste," I never gave it much thought. Probably because all the people admitted were from the war zone of Bosnia-Herzegovina and other war zones before that, before the conflict actually broke out in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Does that mean, Dr. Moljevic, that this book recorded all patients coming in from the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina at that time who were wounded or injured and came to your hospital regardless of how they had been injured; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, mostly yes, and for the most part, they were military conscripts, that is to say, men under the age of 65, according to routine procedure, and also persons injured and with gunshot wounds, whether by bullets or shrapnel or any similar thing. I think that patients who were sick were also sometimes, or all the time, taken in. I could tell you that if I were to look through the whole book, whether sick soldiers were admitted as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You read out, when you read out the person first admitted on the 14th of June, number 186, Simo Vuleta, and I think his diagnosis was not a diagnosis of a wound, but it was a disease; am I correct in saying that? So would you read that out again, perhaps, his diagnosis?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. As I said a moment ago, it says a bleeding ulcer of the duodenum. Yes, that's right, and he was admitted. He was born in 1935 and Vogosca is a suburb of Sarajevo, in fact, and that's why by -- he was automatically inscribed here. I see that another person was injured by a football post, a goal post, and he was sent on to the military medical academy. And then there's another one that I can see, a soldier from Rogatica, in Eastern Bosnia, Territorial Defence, and it says "dermatitis," which means that he has an inflammation of some part of his skin, not to go through the whole book.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: On that same page, would you have a look at number 184, Slavko Tomic from Visegrad? Do you happen to know him personally and is the diagnosis a wound injury or disease, or is it an illness?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I know Slavko Tomic. He is a high medical technician in the health centre of Visegrad and he -- the diagnosis was hypertensioarteralis, which in translation means high blood pressure. He was brought in by an ambulance from Visegrad. The driver was Tesovic Slobodan. And he was admitted into the internal medicine department, but in the column where it says what it is by virtue of his employment assignment or whatever, it says Territorial Defence Visegrad, and he was written into this book automatically.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Doctor, would you look at the 17th of June, whether Nebojsa Kovac and Mitar Vasiljevic, whether they are recorded?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: On the screen I see, it says Mitar Vasiljevic, and I heard you say Mitar Knezevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, doctor. Would you look at the date, the 17th of June.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The number is 203. Admitted was Nebojsa Kovac on the 17th of June, 1992, at 2130 hours. And Knezevic Mitar, the number of that man is 204, also at 2130 hours. In the column, there is a name Markovic Marjan, which was the ambulance driver, whom I know personally and he was killed during the war. So that both were members of the Territorial Defence of Visegrad. Nebojsa Kovac, his diagnosis was vulnus scapuloterium abdomini [phoen], which means a gunshot wound to the abdomen, whereas Mitar Knezevic's diagnosis is vilnus sclepatereo regio ante brace dex [phoen] or, in translation, gunshot wound of the right lower arm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think we'll adjourn now, Mr. Domazet, but I would like to get to the other book if we could when we return. We will resume at 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Moljevic, before we move on to the second book, let us finish with the first one. Would you please turn the smaller book to the 17th of June, where you found Nebojsa Kovac and Mitar Knezevic, who were admitted one after the other. Since we have some additional information of their treatment, would you please have a look at the book and see whether both were entered within the column "admitted," or not?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: In the column where the patient was admitted, Nebojsa Kovac, I have already told you the diagnosis, he was admitted to the shock section. As for Mitar Knezevic, it says that he was returned, which means that he was not eventually admitted to the Uzice hospital. He probably had some light injury.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. You can now move on to the second book. You said that the book includes all the patients admitted during the year 1992. What kind of information -- what kind of data is usually entered into this book?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: May I now open the book, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, yes, please.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Let me see, under "A" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I don't know exhibit number if the Prosecution has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Can you help us?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: No, it doesn't have a prosecution number assigned. I think Mr. Groome has suggested that the Defence is tendering it as an exhibit, so if they want it as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then we would like to tender it, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is there a copy?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It will be Exhibit 33, I should think, but is there a copy of it for us?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That book was never at any point in time in my possession and I suggest that we keep the original as exhibit and perhaps make copies of relevant pages. As far as I know, the book was subject to some expert analysis, as was the other one, but again, it was never actually in my possession. And I could see that it was on the list of exhibits of the Prosecutor together with other documents, hence I believe that it would be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Do you have copy, Ms. Bauer? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't, but we can do one any minute if -- of the relevant pages. I'm not quite sure which are the relevant pages at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, you proceed, Mr. Domazet, and we'll just have to try and follow it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is there any objection to it being an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Then D33 is your next number. Yes, it will be Exhibit D33.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Moljevic, would you be so kind and have a look at the book. Let's see, letter V, since that is the letter we are interested in. Is the book in the alphabetical order listed according to surnames?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the information is entered according -- in the alphabetical order; however, one must bear in mind that we are talking about the Cyrillic script so the letter "V" would be third in order, unlike in the Latin script where it would be somewhere towards the end. Just a moment, please. You wanted me to have a look at the numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Okay. So under the letter V, we have, just as the case with all other letters, the number, then the date of admission, name and surname, and then the fourth column is the department. The first name that we have under letter V is Vinka Vasiljevic, whose personal identification number is 503/92. The date of admission was the 1st of January and the department concerned was ORL, ortholaryngology section.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Dr. Moljevic --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Just a second, please. Here towards the end, we have the date 24th of December, 1992 -- 1991. Those patients were admitted at the end of 1991, but whose information is now entered into 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Dr. Moljevic, do we have the name of Mitar Vasiljevic under letter V?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Ms. Bauer, I can't see both sides of the courtroom at once.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: I just have to apologise, I just discovered and checked the records. It has already been tendered as Prosecution exhibit number 136, so it slipped my attention and everybody else's. So I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, then we can cross it out as Exhibit D33. Thank you very much for drawing our attention to that. It's only numbered that, it hasn't become an exhibit, has it?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: It has been, according to my records, tendered through the investigator Ib Jul Hansen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm quite happy to be proved to be wrong but I haven't crossed it off my list as being admitted as an exhibit. We'll get to checked anyway, but at the moment, we can use document 136 whether it's an exhibit or not. The oracle has spoken. The court deputy says it is an exhibit as P136. You may proceed, Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, maybe it would be good to see if number 137 has also been tendered as a Prosecution Exhibit so as not to tender it once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: 137, certainly has been.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, 137 is the other book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, can you give us the ordinal number?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I don't understand, Your Honour, what ordinal number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, we've got a page of names which I assume is the relevant page. They have a number down the left-hand side which I have assumed, not being able to read Cyrillic, is the ordinal number.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You are talking about the number 136.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And that is the document that the doctor has opened before him now, I'm told. I'm just trying to get to where the relevant issue is rather than read them all out like we did for the last one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Dr. Moljevic, do you have in front of you under letter V the number of the page, the page where Mitar Vasiljevic's data were recorded?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: No, the pages are not marked. What we have is A, B, V, G, D, and so on and so forth, in the alphabetical order but the pages itself are not marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... copies of this document but I am interested for page V. Thank you. I have a copy now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Moljevic, have you found the page?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: What kind of information do we have there?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: On the right side of the book that I have opened under the date 14th of June, in the column which says personal number, we have 10.014, name and surname, Mitar Vasiljevic, department, orthopaedics department.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The other information on the same page, does it concern the persons under the surnames beginning with "V" but the information is of a later date, including the relevant case histories and other data?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I will read out --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Just before you do, Doctor, I wish we could just have a little assistance on this. Is it the first entry on the page?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Because that's the only one I can see for the 14th of June and it looks like 10.014. So the -- what is the left-hand column on that page, what's the heading on it?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Dr. Moljevic, would you please read for us the heading of the column? I assume that we are talking about the column including the numbers.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: The personal number, that is the number under which the patient is admitted to the hospital and we refer to it as the personal admission number.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Is that the number which is included -- which is recorded on the case history of the patient?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The following column is the date of admission; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Then we have name and surname?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you please have a look at the previous page and read for us the name of the last patient before Mitar Vasiljevic, his date of admission and his case history.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: The personal admission number is 10.002, the date of admission 14th of June, name and surname, Simo Vuleta, department, internal medicine department number two.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: So that was the previous patient under the same letter, that is the first letter of the surname whose data was recorded on the previous page?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Dr. Moljevic, so that we are sure about the data and the information here, we have patients whose information was entered in the admissions book and I should like to hear from you the information entered in this book in respect of those patients about whom you have already testified. Let's start with Dragan Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Dragan Filipovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, under "F," can you find Dragan Filipovic, and if so, would you please read his date of admission, personal admission number, and the case history.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I forgot what letter precedes letter "F." I forgot the Cyrillic alphabet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In the Cyrillic alphabet, it is towards the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm glad to see it's as much of a test for the native speakers as it is for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honours. Here it is, I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you please read for us his personal admission number?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: 10.004, the date of admission June 14th. Name, Dragan Filipovic. Department, orthopaedics.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you please turn to letter "L."

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you please try to find the name of Goran Loncarevic and Selim Lepenica.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I assume it would be in April. I think Lepenica should be somewhere in May. Here it is. Personal admissions number 7.869, date of admission May 6th. Name and surname, Selim Lepenica. Department, the shock block, intensive care.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you please look at the Loncarevic information.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Here he is. His personal admissions number is 10.607, June 24th, name surname, Goran Loncarevic, department shock block-surgery.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And one more, please, letter "K," Nebojsa Kovac in the month of June.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Here he is. Personal admissions number 10.247, date of admission 17th of June, name and surname, Nebojsa Kovac, department, surgery. Underneath, we see the shock block or the intensive care, which has been crossed out, and instead, the word "surgery" was written.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You found Nebojsa Kovac in the other book under the 17th of June and Mitar Knezevic was admitted and returned on the same date. Do you see Mitar Knezevic underneath -- under the name of Nebojsa Kovac in this particular book, because according to the previous book, he was returned. He should be under letter "K," Nebojsa Kovac. If he is to be found there, he should be immediately after Nebojsa Kovac. Who is the following patient, the one that comes after Nebojsa Kovac?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: The next patient, the one after Nebojsa Kovac, is the patient by the name of Sladana Kovacenvic, who was admitted on the 18th of June to the surgical department under the personal admissions number 10251. In this book, I don't see the name of Knezevic, nor could you find him there because he was returned. That was the purpose of checking this information in this book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, your witness is behaving absolutely impeccably. He watches the screen and he doesn't answer until the translation is finished, but you have for the last few questions come in a long time before it has finished. Please pause. Just follow your witness's example. He's doing very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're quite right, Your Honour. This time it was my fault. Your Honour, I think that the witness was somewhat confused when he didn't find what he could not have found, but that concludes my questions as regards this book. I should like to check whether Exhibit 537 has been tendered, the smaller book, because I do not seem to recall that the book was tendered into evidence during the Prosecution case. If indeed was the case, I should like to tender it as Defence Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Let me check to see whether it's -- 137 has been admitted. Both of them have an admitted. I did have 137 checked so it's already in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could the witness be shown D32, please? That is the protocol book of the persons who underwent surgery at the orthopaedics.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: My first question for you, doctor, have a look at the book and tell us if you recognise it as being the book from your department and tell us what it contains, please?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is the protocol book for operated patients which contains data about operated patients from January 1991 until mid-August and July, I see here, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you look at the year 1992, the month of June, the 14th, 15th and 16th of June, 1992. I think it's all on one page.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I've found it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you look carefully, Dr. Moljevic, look at the page carefully. I think there are five columns. And would you read out the first column on the page, the date of the operation, who the surgeon was, who was operated and all the rest. What can you tell us by looking at that book and the page?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: This is the protocol book of patients operated at our department. The first column is the ordinal number, that is the ordinal number of this particular patient book. Then you have the personal patient number, admissions number. That number is written down and assigned at the admissions department, and the date the patient was operated. It says here, the next column, it says surname and name of the patient, plus the name of one parent. We very rarely include the name of a parent but I see that is the full title of that column. I never knew we had to write in the name of the parent. The following column is clinical diagnosis. Then we have operation, surgery, and then a brief description of the operative finding and procedure of the surgeon. Then we have operation lasted from to, column 8 is anesthesia, column 9, the surgeon, column 10, the assistants, 11, the anesthesiologist, anesthetics, column 12, and the remarks. You asked about the first column.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And tell us whether it is the patients you talked about today.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: In column number 1, we have the patient who is Filipovic, Dragan from Visegrad, born in 1962. His ordinal number is 283. The personal identification number on the case history is 10004. The date of operation is the 14th of June 1992. The clinical diagnosis is as follows: Vulnus sclapatareum ragio omnus sin cum alvusio acrumioni et column scapulo sin [phoen]. I made a mistake, I said it was the right shoulder a moment ago, but it is a gunshot wound to the left shoulder, in fact, with throw back to the roof and neck of the left shoulder-blade. Operation exploratio vulneris immobilis asio [phoen], which means, in translation, that the wound was examined surgically by means of surgical instruments to ascertain its width, length, and depth. The wound was cleaned from foreign particles -- of foreign particles and bone fractions and other impaired tissue. And that the extremity, in this case it was the arm, was immobilised. And then there is a brief description under operating procedure, what I have just said, actually. Then the following columns state that a local infiltrational anaesthetic was used. The surgeon was Dr. Jovicevic, and under remarks we have the assisting nurse. Her name was Milesa, and the other name was Slobo, who is the plaster cast technician from our department. And together with the doctor, he immobilised the extremity.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Would you look at the next three columns, not to have to read them all. Was it the same day and the same surgeon, the next three columns, and would you read out what it says under number 285, please?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Can we take it in order? 284, Mirjana Popovic, the 15th of June. Her personal admissions number as it says in the book. She was suffering from a fracture of the right lower leg. An extension was performed through the heel bone. Local anesthesia was applied, Dr. Gordic. The next patient, the same day, the 15th of June, Mitar Vasiljevic, a fracture of the left lower leg, the same operation, the same operative procedure and the same surgeon. The same date, same operation date. The patient this time was Rajko Bugarin, and it was the right leg in his case, an extension or -- an extension was performed. The operative procedure wasn't described. This is the surgeon considered it was the same as the previous one. The anaesthetic was the same and the surgeon was the same. Under remarks, the names are different. The plaster cast technician was our department technician and the instruments nurse was a different one this time who was on duty on that particular day, a lady.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could you read out the name of the instruments nurse who worked on the 15th of June, the lady?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: The name is Dragana. I can tell you the surname, Sopalic. She was the only instruments nurse called Dragana at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And now just have a look at the last column on the page, when that operation was performed and who performed it.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Moljevic Andrea was operated from Visegrad on the 16th of June 1992. It was a gunshot wound to the left lower leg where the skin was impaired and the subcutaneous tissue as well as the gastropnemius [phoen] Muscle. The surgeon was myself and it is a patient who is a close relative of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Take a look at that page carefully, please, just one more question. The name of all these five patients, the names are written in different scripts. Tell me, please, which the scripts are for what name. Some of them have been written in the Cyrillic, others in the Latin script. Do you recognise this and is that customary?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: The first column is the Cyrillic script, Filipovic Dragan is one handwriting. Then we come to Popovic, Vasiljevic and Bugarin, that is to say the 15th of June is another handwriting in the Latin script. And the 16th of June is another handwriting, and that is standard procedure, depending on the technician, man or woman, working at our department. When she receives a case history where the surgeon has written his operative findings, it is her duty to record this in the operations protocol book. Sometimes this is done by the head nurse of the department, sometimes it is done by the department nurses which she designates.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, doctor. We have finished with that book now. Now I'd like to ask you to take a look at a copy of the case history.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown document Exhibit P138.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I have a copy in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Take a look at the upper half and tell us whether that is the standard type of printed form that is used and with the information recorded that you spoke about, the date of admission, the personal admissions number for the patient and the doctor whose patient it is.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is the standard type or, rather, the copy of the standard type of case history printed form, the first page, actually. Let me tell you straight away that until -- up until column 11, columns 1 to 10 inclusive, this is filled in at the admissions department. From column 11 onwards, which states basic cause of hospitalisation or in brackets final diagnosis, that is written in by the doctor at the orthopaedic department who is discharging the patient. To make things clearer as to who writes this in, if you are interested, can I go on? It can be written in either by myself as the senior specialist physician who received the patient or, more often, a doctor doing his specialised training or a doctor waiting to undergo his specialist training, which is the most frequent person. That is what most frequently happens because writing down administrative data and seeing to administration under the conditions, our own conditions of work, takes up quite a bit of time. So we senior specialists don't usually waste time on things like that and so it is our -- the younger doctors who see to the administrative side of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Looking at the top left-hand corner above the columns, some information has been written in, not the printed form. Could you explain to us, based on the practice and circumstances of the time, what this is and what it says and why it says what it says?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Let me take this in order, if I may. May I show it on the ELMO so that you can all see? Can I indicate and describe what I'm talking about using the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I think that we all have a copy. You can read it out.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: It's like this, this number up here was 413 and then it was corrected to 411. That is the room the patient was admitted in. I see that the patient was admitted to 413 first and that was a room under Dr. Krnic first but then it was corrected to read 411, which means that the patient was transferred, whether the day or the following day, to 411 and that's a male dormitory belonging to Dr. Jovicevic. 412 is a women's room. We have women's and men's rooms. Underneath, VP is military post, police, so it means who was informed. And I see here 985, the secretariat of the interior was informed, which means in the admissions department they wrote in who was informed, the military police 985 SUP. Now, 386 was probably the number of the room on the psychiatric ward, and next we have the initials of the doctor whose patient it was and we say CDJ, which means Dusko Jovicevic, and then it says case history. And then in capital letters it says injury in the war zone or battlefield in Visegrad, the word is "Ratiste." Now why this was written, I don't know, probably someone in the administration decided to -- that it should be written in this way. I don't know what the next number is, 603/92, I really don't know what that is. Somebody from the administration must have written that in. And I don't know what 05 means.
