The "O" is general hospital Uzice orthopaedics, that is to say that the patient was admitted to our department, the orthopaedics department. The hospital and department, there ought to be some codes there but I've been working in the hospital for 15 years and never have I seen any of that filled in. Then we have the next column, the personal admissions number for the patient, and 3 is the date of admission, 14/06/92 and the personal admissions number I see here is 10.014, 15. I think that the 4 is a stronger digit, typed out more strongly than the 5 digit. The name and the surname, Vasiljevic, Mitar. Ljubisa, in brackets, is the name of the father. I don't know what should be written in there. And then the insurance holder. This is for Yugoslavia. I don't know what happened in Bosnia. Now, if somebody was employed, they would have the name of the company working for. If the person was a farmer, then the holder of the insurance would be the breadwinner, the father of the family. If he was retired, it would say retired. Next, the name and surname of the spouse or parents and address. That column is necessary, should a patient happen to die so that we know who to inform, to come and collect the body or his belongings, or whom we can contact should the need arise, if the patient needs something and the hospital needs to contact his next of kin. Then we have sex, male/female, and then under one, I see one which means male. Two is female. So one is male. Sometimes they circle it in but this says one. Next we have the date of birth, in this case the 25/08/1954. The address or residing in, we usually have the full address written out but here I can see that the address is written next to the spouse so that here it just says Visegrad. 700 UR which used to be the abbreviation for basic organisation of associated labour. That is what it was called in our country. And the technician wrote in "TO," Territorial Defence Visegrad or member of the JNA or whatever. 8, category of health insurance, and we see underlined here Voja Posne [phoen], military post, which means that he was from a military unit of some kind. The employ. For me it would say doctor, for you to would say lawyer, for him, it says reservist. And column number 10, referral diagnosis. That is the diagnosis that appears on the referral letter from the health centre sending it to our hospital. Here it says fractura tibia and fibula one sin [phoen]. This is written by a technician. Technicians don't know Latin as a rule so mistakes are made here. We don't actually take that much notice of that because the main information for us is from column 11 onwards. We write that in, basic cause of hospitalisation or final diagnosis, which is usually the operative diagnosis, so that is the first diagnosis that is written down. It says here fractura cruris L sin, which means fracture of the lower left leg, and the code is 823.2. These are the codes that were used and up until last year. They are old codes. We now use the international code system when Yugoslavia was taken back into the international community of nations and I think that code would now be S 42. something, but that's not essential. That's what it was, a code. This brings us to column 12, other ailments or diseases. In this case, it was psychosis. And this is their code, their old code, probably. And 13 is the date of discharge, day, month and year and the number of days spent in bed at the hospital. Then we have 15, the date and type of operation, it says extensio trans calcanearus [phoen] here, which means an extension via the calcaris, which is the heel bone, and the date when this was done and the year at the end. The outcome of treatment, very often we don't write that in. We don't consider it to be a special obligation. Nobody made us do so. Except if the patient happens to die, then we circle in whether he has had a post mortem examination done or not. Then column 17, the physician treating the patient, in this case Dr. Tesovic, Dr. Slobodan Tesovic. He is a doctor at the psychiatric department who continued the treatment. And for our patients from Yugoslavia, that is, especially those who were injured in a factory, for example, under column 16, "injuries," we would have to say whether the injury was at work or not for insurance purposes, remuneration, compensation, and so on and so forth. So according to the international classification of disease, we would have to write down the code for the external cause of injury, which is column 19, and then we come to column 20, the day and hour of the injury, and 21, rehabilitation. We very often leave that out because they do that in rehabilitation. And if the patient has died, then we are duty-bound to write the cause of death, basic cause of death under column 22. We do this in letters and in code, letters here and code there. It can be a medical diagnosis or it can just be in the Serbian language, a descriptive diagnosis.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. I have just one question for you, doctor, looking at column 20, but before that, let me ask you the following: Do you happen to recall -- I don't think we mentioned that today. Do you happen to recall whether, when you admitted Mitar Vasiljevic or talked to him for the first time, do you remember how he was injured? How did he receive the injuries for which he had come to hospital for?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I learnt about it because the driver, Zivorad Savic, told me that he had fallen off a horse and it would be like this: Everybody else was wounded whereas he happened to fall off a horse, so I remembered that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Could you have a look to see, doctor, whether that -- it's not written in on the first page and my question is why column 20 was not filled out at all, row 20 and column 20, whether it was filled in at that time?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: It depended. With injuries of this kind where you are dealing with fighters or people from another state, which was Bosnia and Herzegovina already then, we didn't regularly write this in. Some people would, but very rarely. As far as I remember, I, myself, didn't fill that column in and as I was a specialist training where doctors who were in training wrote this, we didn't control it. We didn't think it was essential because it says up at the top, injured in the -- on the battlefield. We didn't mind about that very much, so that was the basic heading and we didn't fill the rest in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor. Would you now take a look at the second page, please, and look at the information recorded there. According to you, who wrote that in and was the manner in which the patient was injured recorded there or not?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: This is a typical way, style of Dr. Jovicevic. I write in a similar fashion. Dr. Jovicevic was one of my teachers. I think I can say that, and in the anamnesis and findings, it says admitted to the department as an urgent case which means he wasn't admitted in the morning shift, because of a closed fracture of the lower left leg, which he received falling on a flat plain on the battlefield. He did not lose consciousness. Upon admission, the lower leg was deformed, it had a pathological aspect, active movements are impossible, passive pain, and so on and so forth. Now why he wrote this in, I don't know. I wasn't there when he wrote this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. The next column where it says the 15th of June, are those the same data that you found in the operations protocol book and is it the same number? Would you take a look at that, please.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This data is fully compatible with the data in the operations protocol book.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, doctor. Would you turn to page 3. The rest of the information isn't important for us here. The other witnesses have discussed that. And look at the date, the 17th of July. It is page 4, I think, in your copy. Look at the date, please, the 7th of July, 1992. 17th, 17th of July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: The 17th of July, 1992, it says literally, plaster cast adjusted 16th of July from the orthopaedics standpoint; the patient can be released home. Walking with crutches without reliance on the injured foot. Control examination in one month's time. Tuesday morning, Dr. Moljevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: That was your examination of the patient?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you say, "From orthopaedic standpoint, the patient can be released home," what does it actually mean, because in view of the dates, he was not released on the 17th of July?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: It means that from the orthopaedic standpoint, there is no further need for the patient to be kept at hospital for treatment. Further treatment should be performed by his physician, by the physician who is in charge of him, which was a psychiatrist. I wrote check-up within one month, which means that it is the time when the plaster cast should be readjusted or taken off, depending on the quality of healing, the progress of the healing. Tuesday mornings, in those days, I worked in the outpatient clinic on Tuesdays. The check-up -- and this examination was a consultative examination upon the invitation of the physician who was in charge of the relevant ward where the patient was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Dr. Moljevic, can you remember whether you performed check-ups of Mr. Vasiljevic in this period of his treatment at the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I believe I did. I think I did. Whether it was after the first injury or the second one, I don't know, but I believe that he came occasionally. I don't know whether I was the one who took off the plaster cast. I think that could be seen from the discharge list, the second page of the discharge list.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Dr. Moljevic.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Dr. Moljevic, in connection with this particular case, would you customarily -- oh, I'm sorry, did you ever give a written statement to the Defence counsel of Mr. Vasiljevic?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I gave one statement to you and Mr. Tanaskovic. It was a written statement but I cannot recall the date. I believe that you should have it somewhere. I didn't keep it. I didn't write it for myself and I didn't think it was necessary to keep it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Dr. Moljevic, after that, did you have contacts with the investigators of this Tribunal and did you have any documents with you on such occasions?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think that it was on the 1st of November last year that I received a telephone call of Mr. Yves Roy - I believe that was his name, that was how you pronounce it - following which call I had an interview. I was interviewed in the premises of the IPTF in Visegrad. We spent two and a half, three hours talking. During that interview, I gave a statement in response to their questions. I did have some documents with me, the documents which had been requested by Mr. Roy, since he wanted to have a look at it and to compare it with the copies which were officially issued and certified by the department of my hospital, which you had also requested. I didn't know what you needed at the time. As for the documents that he requested, I was able to see the copies here but also the originals. I went to the archives, and pursuant to an oral approval of the then head of the hospital to collect those documents because I believe that they would be returned, according to what Mr. Roy told me. However, after a very friendly interview, at the very end of that discussion, Mr. Roy informed me that those documents, pursuant to a decision issued by a Judge, I don't remember the exact wording of the decision, I didn't take it and I'm sorry that I didn't take the decision, that such -- that those documents would be confiscated. I can tell you now and I can tell Your Honours here that I was rather worried and concerned about my future status in the hospital. I was very concerned about my future in the hospital because the book here contains 10.000 names approximately, and the small book contains the information about those injured in the war area, and even to this date, many of those who are on this list of names are requesting some -- are seeking compensation either on a private, individual basis or officially or formally because they have lost documentation on their injuries or wounds, and I am telling you this also as a sworn-in court expert, because I am very often required to testify as part of the litigations conducted by the aggrieved against the state. I felt very uncomfortable and I thought it was the same for Mr. Roy as well because we both raised our voices, which was not becoming of the situation and our professions. However, we managed to resolve the differences to a certain extent because I understood that I found myself in the territory of a country which followed certain rules and that I was to abide with these rules. You have these documents now. Judge Hunt, Your Honour, I do believe that this documentation, I hope that this documentation would soon be returned to the country because the situation has changed in the meantime. Laws are much more strict now and I think that it would be high time for this documentation to be returned to the place where it belongs for myself, because of myself and because of the people whose information is contained in this book. I parted with Mr. Roy on friendly terms and we both expressed a wish to meet again, regardless of the circumstances that we found ourselves in on that particular occasion. That's all that I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Dr. Moljevic, do you remember what else, apart from these books that you saw today, what else you brought there on that occasion, what other documents?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: The entire documentation was in a bag that I had with me, and during the interview, this gentleman didn't want me to explain every single detail contained in that documentation. He just wanted to have the documentation at the end of the interview. I remember bringing these books. The protocol book, I'm not quite sure as for the case histories, some information was there. I don't know what exactly was included in the case history documentation, and x-ray findings, and there was also a blank form, case history form dated from the previous year. I don't know why Mr. Roy needed it, but he expressed interest in that so I gave him this particular -- the blank form.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned an x-ray finding as being part of that documentation. I should like you to have a look at it, see whether you recognise it and tell us what it pertains to.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please have the assistance of the usher, but I do not remember the number.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: 151.1, the original, I assume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: It's P151.1, the original

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is that the x-ray? The doctor has referred to the "x-ray findings."

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: I think he meant the x-ray.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's may be so, but that's what he said. Doctor, you are recorded as referring to x-ray findings. Do you mean some report or the x-ray itself, because the x-ray itself is certainly here.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't remember using the word "findings." We do not use the same techniques as in the west, where I also work. I don't remember using the word "findings." X-rays are viewed and examined by us, not by a radiologist. It's not a custom here and those are not the rules. I don't remember using the word "findings." If I did say, I apologise, I must have misspoken or I must have been misinterpreted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's all right, we're just anxious to get the document you want. 151.1, has it been found? That's it. Show it to the doctor, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's how we examine x-rays in Yugoslavia. Mr. Domazet, may I?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: This is an x-ray of a lower leg fracture. A tibia fracture can be observed on the x-ray. Mitar Vasiljevic, 14/06/1992. In the lower left corner, we have a letter L encircled. This was probably written with felt-tip pen. We see the device which was used to immobilise, premer [phoen] wire. Not everything can be seen, only the two-thirds of it. It is an elongated spiral fracture, and since the dislocation is not a big one, it was just split. It is a very bad x-ray, actually, it's been damaged and soiled.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Dr. Moljevic, you recognised a fracture of the tibia, that is the larger bone on this x-ray. You said it was a spiral fracture. On the other hand, you say that you do not see any signs of the fibula fracture, but you are speaking about an upper part that might have sustained this type of fracture. Can you see it on the x-ray? Could you explain that for us?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: [In English] It's no good. [Interpretation] On this x-ray, I don't know whether you can see it. There is an elongated spiral fracture of the tibia. That is the larger bone of the lower leg. And since this is a very long spiral and goes like this, moves upwards, it is logical to assume that there would have been a smaller fracture or a split on the fibula, on the smaller bone. We use the term subcapital. That is below the head or the main part of the shin bone. With these type of fractures, we do not have dislocations in all directions. The fibula is usually cracked, just cracked, so it can heal. Or it may have sustained an insignificant dislocation several millimetres wide, which is not important. The reason why my colleague went for an extension was because that he believed the fibula was also fractured to a certain extent because this type of fracture can be fixed without immobilisation if the fibula was not harmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In this case, according to your opinion, was this x-ray done properly? Could it have been done in a better way? Could it have been taken so as to include what you think is left out?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, Your Honours, ladies and gentlemen, there are many things that are not done in a proper way. In my country, these things happen to this date. Very often, we have to go and see the physician at the x-ray department in person and require for a specific type of x-ray that we need because the staff is not always behaving in the most responsible way; not only in this department, but in any other department. Many doctors do not see any problem with it. However, there is a number of us physicians who have had experience abroad. I spent quite some time at the University of Uppsala in Sweden, working with top specialists in orthopaedic surgery, and I do have a problem with this. However, we have to live with it, such is the situation. I'm not a health minister. I do not hold any position in the hospital where I could undertake disciplinary measures for this type of behaviour, so we're still faced with this type of problem. In view of the relevant rules and regulations in your countries, things that you take for granted, one would have to take an x-ray of the lower leg and the ankle, including the ankle, so one would have a large x-ray or four smaller x-rays so that the doctor would get the entire image, the entire picture. In other countries, there are appropriate procedures, there are possibilities for compensation claims and so on and so forth. However, in our country, things are not done in a proper way. So that is what I wanted to tell you. That is the explanation that I wanted to include in my testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Did we lose some translation there or was there a deliberate pause?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We lost an adage, something to the effect, "It's a long way to Tipperary."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Domazet, are you satisfied with what has been recorded?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dr. Moljevic, you said that in the left corner, you saw a letter L. If indeed that's what it says, could you tell us what it means, does it indicate something and if so, what?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: In the Anglo-Saxon terminology, it refers to -- it means left and in Serbian, it means "levo," which means left.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Does it mean that the x-ray was of the left lower leg?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Dr. Moljevic, you've described for us the fracture of the larger bone, that is the tibia. You said it was an elongated spiral fracture, that is how you described it. Is that type of fracture compatible with the explanation which you have as to the cause and the origin of the injury, that is, the fall off the horse and the relevant side? Is it possible in view of that information for this type of injury to have occurred?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, because the patient when on top of a horse as he lags a stride, so probably one metre above the ground, approximately. In cases of a fall off a horse, the difference is not significant. If he falls off a horse -- as he falls off a horse, his foot touches the ground, the leg turns because of the fall and because of the weight of the body and the fracture that results from that fall is a spiral one in view of the torsion so if the patient falls off a horse, it is possible for the horse to press the leg which is on a flat surface and further fracture would thereby be prevented. However, if the surface is uneven or if you have an uneven body such as a piece of rock or a hard piece of land or soil, then the type of fracture would be different because the pressure of this other body would lead to a new fracture due to the pressure of the horse's body. In this case, it was obvious that it was not the horse, that is, the pressure of its body that caused any additional fracture of the lower leg.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: One other thing, Dr. Moljevic. Do you remember whether Mitar Vasiljevic was a patient at your department in your hospital after this on any occasion after 1992, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Mitar Vasiljevic was our patient for a brief period of time in 1993 less than a year after he sustained this fracture. As to the month, I don't recall but I believe that he was treated by Dr. Krnjic and that no extension was applied, only plaster cast, and he was released from -- discharged from hospital soon after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Dr. Moljevic. This concludes my examination of the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, I think we might start the cross-examination after lunch. We'll adjourn now until 2.30. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.57 p.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Are you part of the team again, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm just here for this afternoon, Your Honour. It always gives me a last opportunity to see Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm not sure how I should take that. Yes, Ms. Bauer.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Moljevic. My name is Sabine Bauer and I'm going to ask you a few questions on behalf of the Prosecution this afternoon. Dr. Moljevic, am I correct in saying that nowhere in the medical record there is any sign of your involvement in the treatment of the accused Mitar Vasiljevic up to the 17th of July, what you have seen so far; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: First of all, let me say good afternoon, to react to your greetings. And in response to your question, you asked me is it not normal or that it is normal or is not normal, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... It is a fact that your name as a treating doctor is not mentioned anywhere on the medical histories or anywhere in the record books as far as we saw them now up to the 17th of July.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. That is customary with us, the patient who -- the doctor whose patient he is, who received him on the ward in the department, his name is written down, but what happens sometimes is that that doctor is absent for any reason, perhaps he is on holiday, and the -- he left before the patient was discharged, say five days before, so it says the doctor whose patient he was, and on the right-hand side, the head of department's name is mentioned. The discharge papers can be written by another doctor. It is usually the doctors doing their specialist training or awaiting to do their specialist training and these doctors are called secondary doctors in our department, as I explained. So as you mentioned my name, I was a doctor on the triage team. I need not be mentioned on the sheet at all because the sheet is written up in the department except for column -- up to column 10.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: So your answer is basically, and I mean what I wanted to get at, as a treating doctor that one could say he was your patient. He wasn't your patient up to the 17th of July for any major treatment orthopaedic treatment, of course, we are talking about only.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: The second part of the question that you asked explains matters for any more important form or major form of treatment. Now let me explain what major treatment means. Us orthopaedists on duty round the clock 24 hours, what is compulsory is the daily round of the orthopaedist. On Mondays, we have the main round, the main doctor's visit with the head of department and all the staff, but after that, it is only the doctor whose patients and the doctor under whom the patients are being treated has his rounds. If he is unable to attend -- to organise the rounds and do the rounds, then somebody else will take his place, but the evening round which is usually between 2000 and 2100 hours is conducted by the doctor on duty that day for all the patients in the department and ward. And also the morning round and evening round is conducted by the doctor on duty if it is a weekend or a national holiday. My name is not mentioned up until the date when I was a consultant, that is to say, when the doctor from the psychiatric department called me. I was probably on duty that day or was called in as a consultant. So I take part in the treatment because at that time, for example, if we look at the number of doctors, I was on duty every five or six days. So by virtue of the job I was doing, I knew all the patients and their problems, why they were lying in the ward.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: So you made control visits but you didn't treat him as your proper patient. Would that be, in summary, correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you told us that you knew Mitar Vasiljevic from beforehand as a waiter, but you didn't have any closer family or otherwise connection with him, did you?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Now, was this customary at that time, Dr. Moljevic, that if a patient from the Visegrad area would come, that they would call you up and say -- because you were from Visegrad, to say there was somebody coming from Visegrad? Was that a customary procedure?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Well, very often, what happened was that apart from the injured person, all the other people, for example, children or expectant mothers, would ask for me because Visegrad is a small town and my family is well-known in town and people say that they are among one of the better doctors. I apologise for having to say so myself. So they ask for me very often because we like to say that if you haven't got anybody you know in a large hospital, you are going to have to wait longer and wait and wait, whereas if you have someone you know, you'll get through your business much quicker. So that this care and attention on my part, when -- and even in other departments when I come in and say I am interested in this patient's treatment, it carries some weight. The patient or the staff would accord a little more attention and pay a little bit more attention to that particular patient.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: So actually, that date in June before Mitar Vasiljevic arrived, you had already been called beforehand, right, because another patient from that area arrived whom you treated, I think it's Dragan Filipovic was his name?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I was chief of the triage team that day and I went to Filipovic and they told me that they had already called me for the Vasiljevic case, that a person from Visegrad had been injured and I should wait for him there, but I was already in the admissions and triage team in the hospital so it was easier for me on that occasion. But there were many other occasions where I had to come from home but that's another matter. I don't want to be sidetracked.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Called you to announce Mitar Vasiljevic's arrival; do you remember that? Who called you, because you said, I think, as far as I see, "Somebody had called me from Visegrad," so I would like to know who called you. If you remember, of course.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I can't remember. A lot of time has gone by since then. They would call me up very often, both friends and relatives, the relatives of the wounded and injured, starting off with their parents, spouses, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. brothers, sisters. So as I say, a lot of time has gone by since then and I really can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Now, you also told us, Dr. Moljevic, that you actually didn't really remember the time any more when Vasiljevic arrived. You said it was sometime in the evening, and in order to refresh your memory, you would have to rely on the records; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: And also, you didn't remember whether he brought an x-ray or whether x-ray tests were ordered or whether any lab tests were done? You can't remember that quite vividly either; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: As far as that is concerned, I, as a doctor in charge of doing the triage for the injured, everything is brought to me and that is something that the GPs who are on duty do. For us in the triage team would just assess whether it was life threatening, whether he was bleeding and whether what he was suffering from was life threatening. Now, we would be told that they were bringing in an urgent patient who was bleeding and so on, which was not this case, but as to what you asked me about the blood tests and the rest, I saw from the documents that this was done in routine form, that they were requested in the morning as a matter of routine. With conditions of this kind where we don't expect to be any major blood loss because it was a fracture of the lower leg, we don't ask for these tests to be done as an emergency measure, but the department doctor is the one who makes the decisions. He decides on what tests, what surgical procedure and so on, depending on the injury. So I, myself, as a triage doctor, in the triage team, I send the patient off where he has to go, whether it is orthopaedics, chest surgery, maxilofacial department or whatever, and then he is taken over there by the doctor on duty in the department and determines the further course of treatment which includes whether additional tests are required, x-rays and so on and so forth. Have I made myself clear?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Yes, you did, doctor. So -- you also, I think you told us that you personally did not fill out any of the admission books but it is the GP, that is, the general practitioner who fills out these admission books; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't think you understood me. It is not the doctor who does that. The particulars are written by a medical technician or one of the nurses working at the administration admissions department. It is not written by the doctor. So in columns where it says "Referral diagnosis," there are very often mistakes in Latin terminology because the medical staff with medium training levels have a poor knowledge of Latin and diagnostics, and that is a valid fact in court. I am a forensic expert myself, a court expert. And so those diagnosis are very often not written correctly because of those reasons.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: And you actually didn't see when these entries have been made, you didn't -- you never see that because it is kept in a separate area, I assume; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see. It's just up to me to decide where the patient is going to be forwarded to and then the technicians wheel him off into a cloakroom where he changes, puts on a pajamas or whatever they have available at that particular moment, and then they take him off to the ward and department that I have sent him to, and those documents are stored somewhere in the admissions department, I don't know, but like what we have behind us here, there are typewriters, there are technicians, they take down the particulars, the relevant information that is typed out on the first page of the case history, and then we have the books like this one here, this big book here and the others ones where these data are recorded in hand. They are written out in hand in the these books.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: So at the first time that you looked for this particular case into this book was, I assume, when you were asked for the records by Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was when Mr. Domazet asked or at the point when -- at the request of Mr. Yves Roy from the Tribunal, took those documents and happened to leaf through and see what it was about, but I didn't study it in depth. I didn't think that was necessary because, in principle, I am well acquainted with the organisation of the hospital services because of the work I do now, that is, I am at the head of the scientific research centre in the hospital, so I am acquainted with some of that. I have to look at literature and case histories from the archives and for the MA thesis that my colleagues do, of which I am the head. I know how that is done. But in 1992, it didn't enter my head. I had just begun to write my specialist thesis for congresses and so on and I would get all those things prepared.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Well, doctor, you told us this morning that you recollect the statement was taken by Yves Roy, and would it recollect to you if you said basically in this statement: It was early in this year, 2000, when I was contacted by Mr. Domazet regarding Mitar Vasiljevic medical records and he said I don't recall the date but he contacted me on my cell phone asking for the documentation for the treatment. So you were first contacted by Mr. Domazet, will you agree to that?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: On my mobile phone, yes. Yes, he came into contact with me first and then in the course of our conversation, he asked me whether I would agree to make a statement before the Tribunal and before the investigator of the Tribunal, and I said there was no problem there, just set the time and place.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: So can I take it that since basically before 2000, you have never tried to take a look at this medical history of Mitar Vasiljevic or at the records? Would that be a correct assessment?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I would say that that is a correct assessment, and with a high degree of certainty -- no, I certainly did not ask for it, I had no reason to.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Now, where would those records -- where were they kept in 1992 in the hospital?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: We have a service for archiving the data, that is to say, the case histories and all the other documentation and usually, in our hospital, it is the last place, if I -- where it should be, if I can put it as candidly as that, using the Serbian language. To the present day, I'm afraid it was stored in the basement. The archives have now been transferred to the basements of certain workshops within the hospital compound. If you were to see where they are actually stored, things would be quite clear to you, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Were those archives moved any time from 1992 to 2000 in these intervening, in these nine years?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I think that a year or two ago, it was transferred from the basement of the -- what we call the new hospital or the surgical block, surgical unit, where there are now warehouses to store humanitarian aid and things that the surgical unit needs, but I think that they're in a basement now and I hear that the facilities are not good today either, but I haven't checked them out.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: And if it would recollect your memory, did you say to Investigator Roy that actually since 1992, these archives were moved three times, to three different locations within the hospital? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Probably, it is. And when I came to the hospital, I seem to remember that the archive was in an old section of the gynecology ward where there was some storage space and then it was transferred to the new hospital wing, and now this final transfer a year or two, or three ago, whenever it was, the latest transfer. Because in -- sometime in 1987, I began preparing documentation to help me write my professional papers and thesis for congresses and that is the work of us younger doctors doing our specialist training, so that the data is sorted according to instructions given me by the senior physicians writing the actual paper. So my work was the work of a research worker and a statistician and he wrote the final text on the basis of the information that I collected, and I think that the archive was in that particular locality but, after all, it was 15 years ago or so.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: And people like nurses or doctors, if they wanted to check a record, they did have access to these records, correct, if they had to go back for any kind of reason?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: You mean personally, to go to the room personally?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: At archives, yes.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, there's no need for that because there are archivists, five or six people, men and women working in the archives. We just send the names and surnames and the time when they were hospitalised, and then they can look through the archives and find what we need and then they would bring it up to the orthopaedic ward to the doctors' room, the case history we had requested. That's the usual procedure. There's no need for the nurses to go and look for it and nor is that their job, if you understand me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: And the -- you said if you wanted to take out the books, you know, the whole books, the ledgers, you had to ask permission from the director. Was this across the board? Is this sort of a rule for everybody or was this just in this particular case that if you needed to take out the book for whatever purposes?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, this is a case which is a little unusual and I have no need to take a book out. If I want something, I need a case history, so if you're asking me as a doctor, if I need something for a congress or for a specialist paper. Now, as far as the other data required from these books, we doctors don't need that. The patients come to ask for that or the relatives of patients. If, for example, they have died, for certain rights to be -- to get a certificate from our hospital saying that they had been hospitalised from such and such a time, or if they have lost their discharge papers, then that is photocopied, or letters, and it is photocopied but it has an official stamp of the legal department of the hospital, certifying that the copy is true to the original. That's what can be done, but we didn't have to go. I don't need the book. I don't see why I would need it. And in this particular case, as I had to go to another country, to Bosnia-Herzegovina in this instance, to show Mr. Yves Roy the original of what he already had photocopied and in front of him. He said he would look at it and give it back but the then director of the hospital gave me oral permission to take it out with me and the archives were instructed to hand me over those documents but unfortunately, we saw what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Now, when you took out those books, were you asked actually to bring the complete case file of Mitar Vasiljevic or did you make a selection based on any kind of criteria?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Who do you mean asked me? You did, your investigators or any lawyers? Who do you -- who are you thinking of, who do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: We agreed before that Mr. Domazet first asked you to get hold of these documents. Now, I wanted to know when you got these documents, did you simply go out and get the whole case file of Mitar Vasiljevic in 1992, and 1993, whatever you could find in the archives, or did you make some kind of a selection?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I see. Well, I looked downstairs in the room where the archive staff are. I didn't say that. I didn't -- they wouldn't allow me without having a written permit stating why I needed -- I just took a look at what it was about. I looked in the case history. I'm not certain which of these books was given to me and I didn't ask. I think that it was probably the big admissions book and the admissions book for the wounded because that's -- those are the books where you would find that kind of data. I didn't ask for any other books until Mr. Roy told me what kind of documentation he needed, and then once he did that, we started working on the case as far as literature, administration, books and documents were concerned.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: We talked about the two admissions books. As far -- I think we had in the beginning a difficulty but as far as I understand, the big book was the general admission book for everybody in the hospital, and the small book only about basically soldiers, war casualties or soldiers being fallen sick; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm not sure that that is --

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you've understood that correctly. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Let's get our books straight. This morning we had two books there, the big book and the thin book, and the thin book was those from the war zone. Some bright person thought of the title, the doctor told us. Are those the two books you are talking about there?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But it was a little bit broader than just people who were soldiers, I thought he said.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Well, I think there was a reference to military conscripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, but not restricted to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We'll go back and look it up if you are concerned about it but he said, the doctor told us that somebody in the administration thought up the title "war zone" for this thin book.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Well, then could the witness please be shown the Exhibit 137.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I answer the question that you asked me? What you said was right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Well, exactly, that's the small book?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Now, do you have the copied pages of Prosecution Exhibit 135? Yes, you have it. Now, if you would look at the last column. Apart from one entry, will you agree with me that everybody seems to be from a TO, from a military unit? I think the copied page is also in front of you. It should be the same so ...

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's a little clearer to me here so I'll take it from that there. You asked me whether it says Territorial Defence for most of them, for the majority. Yes, or reservist. That would be the other term. And for the last column, and that's what you were asking me about with the patient Radoslav Jovicevic, born in 1963 in Ljubovija, the diagnosis is [Latin phrase] which means both lower arms and the right side of the back in the shoulder-blade region. The driver was Zavic Dragoljub from Bratunac, a private vehicle being used as an ambulance. Admitted to orthopaedics, it says here the Serb volunteers unit. Now what are you interested in?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: No, actually, what I was interested in and basically you answered my question, that most of these people written in this ledger were somewhere militarily active, correct? So one could say they were soldiers, whether they incurred an injury actively fighting or just being sick is a different matter that's then in the diagnosis but they were soldiers in the small ledgers, principally?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: You have given the answer yourself. Let me add not just soldiers, but military-age men, the conscripts. In the former Yugoslavia and in the former Bosnia, military-aged men were all males up to the age of 65.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: And that would be also the reason why one of the persons that have been informed when something happened to these people is the military police would be informed; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, do you recall you looked at the x-ray you were shown this morning and you told us that you saw just one fracture because the x-ray, according to you, didn't show more than that; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Yes, you are correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: And you explained to us that such a spiral fracture could occur from falling on to -- from a horse; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: But it wasn't the horse's weight that, in reality, incurred the fracture; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: [In English] No.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Not correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: No, it was not the horse's weight because first, he broke his leg and then the horse leaned on him.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: So would you agree with me that if somebody would slip on a slope and fall down on a hard surface, also such a fracture could occur?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Your knowledge of medicine is quite good.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, doctor, you somehow admitted that basically many of the records, including the x-rays, are not quite to the standard you personally would expect, that there are mistakes and that x-rays are not recorded correctly; is this right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: And since the events or since these records have been moved occasionally and nine years have been passing by since the events, would I be correct that it could also be that they are not 100 per cent complete, that simply things are missing?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Very often, some x-rays are missing, not only x-rays but also findings of blood tests, findings following surgeries which are entered on a separate form by anaethesiologists and not by us surgeons, that is the beginning of the operation and the operation itself and the period following the operation, the amount of blood given to the patient, any other liquid solutions given to the patient during the surgery, the amount of antibiotics given during the operation and all other medicines that are administered to the patient during the operation. For example, in cases of blood failure, special medicine is administered and so on and so forth. So that kind of information is sometimes lacking and we have the same problem in every aspect of the society, economy, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Thank you, doctor. I'd like to look at Defence Exhibit 32, the operations log, please.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: If you could look, please, at the last column, "Remarks."

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Now if I ask you to look at the ordinal numbers 284, 285 and 286, all got an operation which sort of led to an extension, or as we call it here traction; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Just a second, I am looking at this list but at random, I'm not looking at any particular number. Do you want me to see the portion concerning Vasiljevic's operation?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Yes, and the one before, 284 ordinal number and the one 286, and the question was whether you wouldn't agree that it was sort of the same kind of operation was performed, namely, that these people were getting traction or an extension applied to?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Just a second, let me find the page. Yes, I have the page in front of me. 284, Mirjana Popovic from Ivanice [phoen], born in 1945, female. It was not a surgery, properly speaking; it was an intervention. However, that is also entered in the operations protocol. It is a rule which we've had for I don't know how long. [Latin phrase] which means that a bone traction is applied and it is from 2.58 millimetres -- up to 8 millimetres long and it is applied through the bone. The so-called bridle is applied, which is usually 10 per cent of the patient's weight.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. That is very interesting detail but we don't need to be so detailed, I'm afraid. What I wanted to know is that if you look at those, basically numbers 284, Popovic, Mirjana, 285 Mitar Vasiljevic, and 286, what I just want to know, if they had the same kind of operation or measure applied to them. That was my question; correct, extensio transulnaris [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I do apologise for the digression, I'm not -- I won't do it again. These three operations are the same except that in the third one, we have extensio taloclorois [phoen], which is just an old term for the same type of traction because the traction could not be performed through the ankle because the damage would be even greater than the one caused by the fracture. No traction is ever performed through the ankle bone, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Well, and then you told us that basically the instrument nurse was Dragana, correct, and I think that you've seen -- in column number 3, right? And the plaster cast technician was a person called Milovan. Do you remember having said this this morning?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Not Milan but Milovan, it's a man's name. And the name of the lady here who was Dragana, Dragana Sopalovic. As for Milovan, I cannot remember his surname. Dragana Sopalovic is a nurse and she is currently working the protocol in our outpatient clinic, so I know who the person is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: But see, doctor, what I don't quite understand on this protocol, and I'm going to be quite outright, you told me that all these three operations were basically the same. Then it appears that in one, the plaster cast technician, in two, plaster casts were applied and with Mitar Vasiljevic's entry, the plaster cast technician wasn't there. So though it was the same operation, how come although at one point the plaster cast is there and only with Mitar Vasiljevic he wasn't there? Could you explain that, please?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Of course I can. You misunderstood. When you apply traction, you do not apply plaster cast. You apply plaster cast only sometime later on, after two or three weeks' time, so you don't quite understand what we're talking about. As for the plaster cast technician, it is a person, a technician who is in charge of preparing the instruments needed for the traction. One of such instruments is the Brownbeller's [phoen] machine, where you put the leg on. He also prepares the stirrups and other necessary instruments. The instrument nurse in this case was Dragana. She's the one who would have brought the Kirschner pin and various types of Kirschner pins and the surgeon is the one who selects the right type of Kirschner pin to be applied, and all other medical material, bandages, various other instruments all properly packed and sterilised. The surgeon, meantime, gets ready. He has to clean up the area that is to be operated, and then when the surgeon drills a hole, the technician is holding the stirrups. It is a quite painful procedure. The location itself is not very painful but it is the fracture that causes the pain. The plaster cast technician is the technician in charge. He is the one who does it, not the nurses.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: So how come then that if he is the technician to prepare the traction and all three operations were the same, why is his name not mentioned in column 13, if you look at it?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: It's just an example of negligence. Milovan is not important. Dragana is not even important as far as professional responsibility is concerned. It is the surgeon who is the responsible one. The other staff are replaceable.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: So you would agree that the record is again incomplete; right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I wouldn't say that the record is incomplete. It's just that it was not done with due diligence, if I can put it that way, in accordance with customs prevalent in my country.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, let me ask you something else. Since you were from Visegrad, I assume that during the war, you tried to keep updated with the developments in Visegrad; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is quite right. That was my moral and professional obligation. Moral as their fellow citizen, fellow resident, and a professional one because I was one of the most senior surgeons at the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, did you hear in the summer of 1992 about the fire which killed 65 Muslims? Did you hear about that through some means or other?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I heard about that after the arrest of Mitar Vasiljevic because up until the end of July 1992, I was at the hospital and was subsequently engaged in the military corps elsewhere for a while. And I also read about it in the press, but after the arrest of Mitar Vasiljevic. But I didn't much inquire about the incident neither with other citizens nor with my family members.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Now, to summarise, Doctor, is it correct that basically eight years ago -- in 1992, you were first -- in 2000, I'm sorry, you were first asked to recollect events from eight years ago, from 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that was the first time by Mr. Domazet, that is the Defence counsel, and then by Mr. Roy and his team.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: And in the meantime, in those eight years, I'm sure I'm correct that you probably had thousands of patients that you treated and you saw and you operated on, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that is absolutely correct. I had -- I operated on 712 wounded persons but as a surgeon, generally speaking, I have so far performed over 2.100 operations, including the wounded.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: And at the time, wartimes, you also told us you were very, very busy and you got a lot of patients from all over the country and the war zone; correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, because I was one of the surgeons who also performed the so-called secondary operations, that is the reconstructions of operations that had been performed earlier on in the war area. That is the usual custom, anything that required a more complex surgical intervention later on. I wrote three papers on that issue which have been published in the mean time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: And to summarise, I mean you don't have any independent recollection of a single day eight, nine years ago, without relying on records on the medical files?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: You're right. Yes, you're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Moljevic, I have no further questions for you at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Dr. Moljevic.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Just a few questions that have arisen from the cross-examination by Ms. Bauer. In response to one of her questions as to whether this type of wound can occur if a person slips on a slope and falls down on an even surface, you stated that it was indeed possible. Now, I should like to know whether that can cause a spiral type of fracture, and if so, how is it that such a fracture is possible. Can this fracture be caused by any fall or do other conditions have to be met for this type of injury to have occurred?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: I see. Both Madam Prosecutor and yourself, you mentioned the case of slipping. That immediately, in my mind, means a spiral type of fracture, because I have many years of experience. A fall on even surface without fracture, on flat surface, that causes simple fracture of an ankle. However, with slipping, it is logical for the weight of the body to be placed on the one side of the body, causing torsion, and between -- it is between the lower third and the mid-third of the lower leg that the fracture would occur. Slipping immediately brings into mind a spiral fracture; however, you mentioned a fall on flat surface. If it is without slipping, that type of fall would cause the fracture of an ankle. However, if there was slipping as well, it would mean that the weight would be concentrated on the mid-and lower third of the lower leg and that the pressure was applied to that particular part of the lower leg, causing fracture.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would that be the case causing the so-called spiral fracture?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: One of the questions of Ms. Bauer was -- or rather concerned your activities towards -- your treatment of Mr. Vasiljevic. Apart from the 17th of July, whether you did anything in particular with him. You explained to us the system of rounds carried out every Monday where the whole department is inspected and you also spoke about the system of duties. My question in relation to that was whether you went to see him outside these regular visits that you have spoken about that took place in this period of time?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Domazet, I mentioned in response to a question by Ms. Bauer that it was my moral obligation to pay more attention to my fellow co-residents, so I went to visit other people from my area in addition to Mr. Vasiljevic, to ask them whether they needed something, cigarettes, cakes, and things like that. So that is what I did and I believe that it was the right thing to do because it is much easier for a patient when they -- when he or she saw me and not somebody else and they were happy to see me outside my regular duties, perhaps happier than -- to see other persons paying them visits.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you spoke about the system of duty shifts, you said that in view of the number of the physicians, you were on duty every fifth or every sixth day, every five or six days. The way I understand it is that you were on duty the fifth or the sixth day and that you would be on duty in the third shift, in the second and third shifts. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can be even more precise. Just bear with me a little. Dr. Milo Safljevic was never on duty because he was ill and then it was Stojkovic and Vasiljevic and myself. We would be on duty every fifth day and then sometimes on national holidays -- we had specialists for duties on national holidays because that duty shift would be paid separately.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The reason why I'm asking you was because the transcript read, "I was on duty every five or six days" so I was afraid that there would be a misunderstanding. However, you are telling us now that it was the special type of duty, duty shift, but normally, you worked in the first shift as all other physicians; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you're correct. We worked, of course, every day except when it was my turn to be on duty, then I would be on duty 24 hours but the next day would be a day off for me. However, in view of the general situation and the great influx of the wounded in some periods of time, most of us never used that day off because pursuant to an order of the director of the hospital, the time off was regulated in a special way in those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Dr. Moljevic, Ms. Bauer asked you about the way the records were kept and to what extent they were kept in a proper and adequate way, and you were quite critical when you spoke about the way that job was performed. I should like to know whether you have had cases of mix-up of x-rays? Did you have errors of that kind like erroneous names, mismatches and things like that? Were such errors possible as well? I'm referring to the relevant times but also as general practice.

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, to be quite frank, the problem didn't only concern those days. We have the same problem today. Very often, the sides of the hip x-rays are switched, but it is easy to deal with in cases of a different gender of the patient, the different sex of the patient, but we do have such problems. Because I would receive an x-ray per purported to be an x-ray of a male patient and I could tell it from the x-ray that the patient was female. Such problems are common not only in our country but elsewhere in the world. I'm interested in these problems and I've read he had about it on the Internet. Such incidents are relatively common everywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Dr. Moljevic, did the way in which these records, these entries, were made contribute to that when the x-rays were developed or do you have an explanation of your own as to how these mistakes were possible?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, let me say again in one sentence, a great deal of negligence and irresponsibility that prevails everywhere in the parts we come from today and the impossibility of sanctioning such behaviour or a lack of will to exert sanctions for things of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. And that brings me to what I think will be my last question. Ms. Bauer asked you whether your recollection of these events, especially the day on which Mitar Vasiljevic was admitted, whether you relied on the documentation and you say that you remember the date and even the day of the week on the basis of that. But you also gave us other data such as the visit to Dragan Filipovic which probably stems from your memory; am I right?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Are you sure, Dr. Moljevic, that Mitar Vasiljevic was admitted the same day as Filipovic Dragan was admitted, whom you mentioned and said you had visited?

utterances.speaker: ALEKSANDAR MOLJEVIC
utterances.text: 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor, for coming along to give evidence and for the evidence which you have given. You are now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Judge Hunt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You better be careful, doctor, she might take some of your documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I should tell Your Honour, I was present when the doctor was interviewed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I knew that. You should have been here when he gave us the description of it this morning. Now, Mr. Domazet, let's see where we stand. You are concerned about Dr. Stojkovic. He, of course, is the doctor whose name appears most often on the records but do you think his evidence is really going to add to what we've already got and, if so, how?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, I do not think that it -- we could get something new through his testimony. It is true that he is one of the witnesses who -- one of the names who appears on the discharge certificate with his own remarks and signature, and as the Prosecution questions were always frequently directed towards whether witnesses had written down something in person, I really did consider that the witness was necessary and would have liked to have seen him here. However, if we come to the conclusion that after all the testimony we have heard to date, that is not necessary, although I personally would have liked to have heard him, I could agree to not calling him and not listening to his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I want to make it very clear though, Mr. Domazet, I'm not suggesting that at all. I'm just curious to know whether you think that he will add to the fund of evidence we've got. The last time I asked the Prosecution about its case, they were still maintaining that your client was never in the hospital. Oh, yes, you were. If that is no longer the Prosecution case, then let us hear you say it, Ms. Bauer. If you remember, I asked Mr. Groome whether the only issue which remained was what time and day did he get there and he said that the Prosecution was still relying upon the evidence of Dr. de Grave it could not have been the same person. Now, if that's changed, I wish we'd have known several week ago because we've heard an awful lot of evidence which goes to demonstrate that he was in the hospital.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Your Honour, you're correct, we still challenge that he was there at that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: No, that's not the question I put to you. Is it still the Prosecution case that he was never in the hospital in June and July 1992? If you don't want to answer it, I can understand the problem that Mr. Groome is not here but it becomes important as to whether it is necessary to call yet another doctor to say that they saw him there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: I wouldn't like to really jeopardize or preempt Mr. Groome's assessment of the situation after he has heard the last few witnesses, or read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: When will Mr. Groome be returning?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: I just was told today that I will return only on Wednesday. I mean if Your Honours so wish, I could ring him up and say whether he -- whether I can put on the record whether we uphold the position that he was never there in June or July of 1992 or whether the position has changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think it might be a very good idea. I am not making any prejudgment at all, but the only evidence that you have got to demonstrate that he was never there is the evidence of Dr. de Grave. Now, that has been, on the basis of the x-ray, could not have been of the same person. And we've got a report, a rather sketchy one which the Prosecution properly handed on, and then a more detailed one from the Defence which I assume we're going to hear from the doctor but nevertheless, there is at least an explanation put forward as to why the x-rays taken this year would be unlikely to show an injury such as was caused or said to have been caused to Mr. Vasiljevic and demonstrated by that x-ray that's been handed around today. I don't want to suggest that I have made up my mind one way or the other, but it is no longer the clear-cut case.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: May I just intercede one second? We have another expert, actually, who is the third or fourth expert one way or the other. He is the fourth expert, actually who, as far as I can say now, supports the results of Dr. de Grave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All right. Well that will produce an issue and no doubt then I can guess what Mr. Groome's reaction will be, he will say it is still part of the Prosecution case that Mr. Vasiljevic was never in that hospital during June and July, and if that's so, well, then I'm afraid we will have to see what's going to happen about Dr. Stojkovic. Well, Mr. Domazet, when will Dr. Stojkovic be available? Last time I asked you, you said he couldn't be here this week. And we are sitting on Monday and Tuesday next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think, Your Honour, I don't think we're working on Tuesday because of the Milosevic case, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I told you that we definitely would be sitting on Tuesday, that the security had accepted that we were so hidden from public view here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I talked over the phone with Dr. Stojkovic last night. He is unable to come this week or next week and that's where the problem lies. So that if he were to give testimony, that could only be the first day when we continue sitting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And is he your last witness of this type? We've got a psychiatrist to come yet and your expert radiologist, but is he the last of the witnesses about the hospital?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, with respect to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, when are we going to see your expert on the x-rays?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the x-ray expert, I haven't received the Prosecution's viewpoint, whether they wish him to be heard. If so, we will try when we can, but the problem with that expert witness is when he will be given a visa because it was requested and my information says that it was sent off to the Ministry but that it has not come back to Belgrade yet, that is to say, guarantees for the visa and that's the problem attending that particular witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, you will probably be very tired of me repeating this but this has been an issue in the case since early this year - I thought it was the end of last year, but let's say it was early this year - as to whether or not this x-ray supports or destroys your case. Now, the efforts you have made to get an expert appear to have started sometime last week or the week before and I am wondering whether this is just sheer inattention or whether there's some plan to it. I don't understand why it has been left so late. When was his visa sought?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same day when the request was made for the registrar to allow the expertise and time -- that same day the request was made, and I can also tell you that unfortunately, another expert witness, who is an elderly man, a retired professional, was to do this but then said he couldn't. So I had to change my expert witness, which led to the delay and the problems that arose. It should have been a Mr. Radulovic, who was to have been the expert witness but he had some problems. He's an elderly man. So I had to change my expert witness and find somebody else who I have never met personally, and that is what set me back. We had to find him in Belgrade and then go ahead with the procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure why you had to find him in Belgrade but nonetheless, I suspect I see a reason for it. But whose report have we got, your first expert or your second expert?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean the other one, yes, the second one. The other one didn't do that, but Dr. Cedomir Vucetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I haven't got it in front of me so I don't know. The only report you've filed is that of your most recent expert; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, the orthopaedic report was handed over before this, last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's the one that deals with the x-rays.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the report by the orthopaedist relates to the -- an examination of the x-rays which the expert did look at. Mr. Groome gave me copies, which I sent to Belgrade, and he looked at the copies and he makes his findings, that is that testimony expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And now you're saying there's going to be another x-ray expert to give evidence, is there?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I'm not sure we understood each other, Your Honour. It's one and the same. The one that made his report and findings, not another one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, have you any idea when we're going to get him here?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as he himself is concerned, he can come as soon as he receives his visa and the other travel authorisations, but we have had very poor experience with the duration for the visa. I had the problem that Mr. Tanaskovic, prior to this trial, received his visa just one day prior to departure although it had been requested for a month beforehand, so that visas are always a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, let's just see what the Prosecution says now formally about this last report we've received.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Your Honour, you mean now the x-ray report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: We would like to cross-examine the expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Right. Well, then you have to bring him, Mr. Domazet. What about your psychiatrist?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I handed over today the psychiatric report, according to our agreement. I left a copy on Saturday evening for Ms. Bauer and today officially handed it over to the Tribunal and I'm waiting to hear from the Prosecution whether the -- they will be cross examining the psychiatrist too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, I can understand that you wouldn't have an answer just yet, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Well, I'm fairly positive we will want to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
