utterances.text: All right. Very well. Well, when can she come?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as she is concerned, and as far as the -- she's already been to The Hague so I don't think the visa is the problem. All we have to do is find a slot for her here. She personally, although she has devoted more than a week to this case, she came to The Hague and then wrote her report, when I asked her, she asked me, if possible, that she be not asked to come just now in the next few days because she is teaching at university. She has her student courses. So -- but I will contact her if it is a problem and try to see if the -- I should like to hear from the Prosecution when they would like to have her for the cross-examination and then I could ensure that she be here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, I don't think you quite realise where we're at. You have run out of evidence. Now, I'm trying to work out how to get your witnesses here. You are meant to call a witness tomorrow. You don't have one here. So we've got to work out how we get them here. It's not a question of when the Prosecution wants them here for cross-examination, it's when you can get them here to give their evidence. The Prosecution, provided they've been given sufficient warning, just has to fit in.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. So that was my question. I was asking the Prosecution when it will be ready, and I will try and have the expert witness here for that day in view of the time table that the Prosecution had at its disposal. I didn't dare take on the responsibility of bringing this expert witness now, in these few days, because we've only just handed over the report, so I didn't know whether the Prosecution would be ready.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I mean, we are just in the process of identifying an expert that could at least take a look at the report and conduct maybe an examination of the accused himself so until we have hopefully identified them by tonight or tomorrow at the latest, I don't think we are sort of ready before this person has read the report at least to cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I understand that but then this has been something I have been badgering Mr. Domazet about for the last week, and you mean you haven't yet even retained a psychiatrist.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: We have contacted several psychiatrists but, in fact, of that it would probably be preferable to have a native speaker. It seems to be not that easy to get hold of one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, then, do you think that we will be able to know where we're going tomorrow morning?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: I hope so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, so do I.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: I'm going to make the necessary inquiries but I only can say I tried last week 100 times to call a name in Croatia and I never got through so...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: If I had been you, I am afraid I might have tried somebody else if I had sat there 100 times, but anyway, it seems that the parties here are taking a very relaxed view about the problems we have in finishing this case, which leads me to this: Mr. Domazet, the Prosecution has been slowly building up a case in reply. I don't know how many witnesses will be involved, but the number of loose ends in this case because you were not able to cross-examine the Prosecution witnesses have grown exponentially during the course of the case. Can you see any particular problem if we reserve the rest of your case and allow the Prosecution to start calling its witnesses in reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, would that mean that I cannot present my evidence because in that case, I really couldn't accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think you've misunderstood me. I said if we reserve the rest of your case so that you can call it, and if something arises in it, the Prosecution will probably still have to call evidence in reply, but there are a number of factual issues which have been raised in your case which were not put to the Prosecution witnesses, and the Prosecution, as I understand it, is proposing to call evidence in reply on those issues. It will mean the evidence being called out of order to some extent, but bearing in mind, if I may put it as kindly as I can see how, this all results from your failure to be ready, I'm asking you whether you see any particular problem in allowing the Prosecution to call some of its factual witnesses in reply and you can call the remainder of your case when we can finally get your witnesses here.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, that is possible, but I think I should be informed as to what the Prosecution intends to prepare in its reply so that I, too, in my turn, can prepare. Otherwise, I have nothing against if we would gain time that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's certainly fair enough. I'm surprised that they haven't given you anything yet. What's happening about the Prosecution's case in reply, Ms. Bauer? I was told by Mr. Groome that it would last a week, which rather horrified me but, nevertheless, that assumes that you have a number of witnesses and I assume you have statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Unfortunately, Mr. Groome didn't really identify me about his sort of plans who were the people he intends to call. I have a rough idea, but I really couldn't answer this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You mean that Mr. Groome can't produce any statements either?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: I mean I haven't seen personally one that I could produce now so far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The doctor this afternoon was talking about something called blood pressure, and I'm afraid mine is rising. I do not understand how if this has been going on for so long, the Prosecution hasn't been prepared for it. What has been going on? I know Mr. Groome has got himself involved in another case which seems to be his prime concern and that we play very much a second fiddle, but I am getting, if I may say so, a little irritated that we are being left so far behind when he knows the real problems that we face. If we do not finish this case in the first two weeks of next year, then there will be grave problems about trials that have been fixed to start because there simply aren't the courtrooms to run more than six trials at once, and this will be the seventh. Now, I think that we are entitled to know what is going on and I realise that Mr. Groome isn't here and it's a personal matter, and we don't wish to blame him for not being here at the moment, but that was something which I understand arose very late last week and I would have expected that there would be something on the way by way of statements so they can be served on Mr. Domazet so he can be ready to cross-examine them. So when you speak to him, I think you better get some details and ask him in which drawer of his desk he has kept these statements from us, and I suggest that when you have spoken to Mr. Groome, you contact Mr. Domazet and put him in the picture as well so that tomorrow, we will know a little bit better about where we're going. Now, there is one other or two other matters I want to raise. I don't know if it has ever been formally stated in court, Ms. Bauer, as to the results of the testing that was done by the Prosecution on these documents. They were given leave to test certain documents that were seized. For example, I'd be interested to know whether document 137, which was the thin book, the so-called war zone book, was one of those which was tested. Do you know?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: I think that's correct, both books were tested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, I'd like to have that properly confirmed in the morning, and that the Prosecution is not able to challenge the genuineness of the documents. I had always understood that 136, the very big book, was the one being tested but perhaps you could tell us tomorrow whether 136 and 137 were the subject of those tests and the Prosecution is unable to challenge their genuineness. That's one matter. The other matter, Mr. Domazet, is for you. Your client was asked when he was giving evidence why Dr. Jovicevic, I'm sorry, the doctor who admitted or signed the document admitting your client, was not on the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. witness list and he said words to this effect, he has to have some spinal surgery and that we should ask you about it. We are asking you about it, what is the position about that doctor?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my information is that he's on sick leave. He was to have had an operation on his spine. I don't know whether he has had the operation yet, and it was only for these health reasons that he personally wished to be exempt from coming here and testifying. I can make inquiries if you consider that that witness's testimony would be important if he would not be able to come here, perhaps by videolink, but that was the only reason he gave me, his health. That was why he asked not to be called as a witness, because he felt that a sufficient number of the doctors from the hospital had already come to testify. So that was the only reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I don't intend this in any way as a comment but you do understand that whilst we have today's doctor saying he saw him at the time, this particular doctor is the only one who actually signed something to say that he saw him on that particular day, and if the case comes down to an issue of not was he there but when did he get to the hospital, obviously, this doctor's evidence is significant. Now, it may be that a videolink would have to be dealt with next year at this stage. We can't send anybody out within the next few days. They do take some time to organise. But either that or if he's not going to be called, we would need something more than either triple hearsay from your client or double hearsay from you; in other words, some sort of a medical report saying he's unable to travel. But it is, if I may say so, an issue which could very well arise in the case because if your expert on the x-rays casts some doubt upon Dr. de Grave's evidence which, on the report we've got, it tends to do so, then the issue is going to be not when he was in hospital but when did he get there as being the vital issue in the case. Whilst you bear no onus of proof, only you can produce the evidence which will demonstrate the Prosecution case has failed. I emphasise, I'm not suggesting you bear any onus of proof at all, but it's just a question that the only person who can produce that evidence would be you. That's a matter for you, it's how you deal with it, but it is a matter that I suggest you should give some careful consideration to. Where inferences can be drawn about failures to draw witnesses, and I'm not saying that they are available here or not, that's something I haven't really had to work out, but to meet any such inference, at the very least, some sort of medical report would be vital. All right. Well, now, tomorrow we are due to start at 9.00 in the morning, I remind you, because we are sharing the courtroom with the Appeals Chamber, I think, because of some terrible mix-up in the registry. So we'll start at 9.00, and it doesn't look as if it's going to be a very long day, but I think we'd better, having arranged 9.00, start at 9.00. So we shall see you in the morning. We will adjourn now until 9.00 a.m. ---Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 4.03 p.m. to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 4th day of December, 2001 at 9.00 a.m.
